item.title: Improvement: Drupal installer flaws SA-CORE-2026-017 and -019 exploited; update to 11.4.14, 11.3.23, 10.6.23 and run update.php
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-136716 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-27 on evidence of active exploitation it does not describe, so the entry's statement that the newer flaw was not on the list no longer holds; Drupal already reported the flaw exploited.
item.content:encoded:
Improvement28 Nov 2026 07:33 UTCrun 2026-11-28T0355Z-intelcvessourcesevidencebody

CISA added CVE-2026-136716 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-27 on evidence of active exploitation it does not describe, so the entry's statement that the newer flaw was not on the list no longer holds; Drupal already reported the flaw exploited.

CISA added CVE-2026-136716 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-27, in an alert that says the additions rest on evidence of active exploitation and does not describe that exploitation, so the statement in the 2026-11-26 section that the newer flaw is not on the list no longer holds (CISA, 2026-11-27). item.title: SAP confirms suspicious activity; GitHub, Project Granite and token theft reported; no customer-data access found
item.description: SAP told dpa and BleepingComputer on 2026-11-26 and 2026-11-27 that it identified suspicious activity, took measures to protect customers and has found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data; a letter that dpa saw in part places the activity in SAP's GitHub developer platform. DER SPIEGEL's insider reports, without SAP's confirmation, stolen employee authentication tokens and copied and possibly modified source code, and heise, relaying Handelsblatt's company circles, reports restricted GitHub access, paused development workflows and replaced signing keys. SAP has not said how the attackers got in, who they are, or whether any software delivered to customers or any signing key customers verify is affected.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

SAP: suspicious activity in its GitHub development platform (Project Granite), with reports that employee authentication tokens were stolen and source code copied or modified; SAP says it found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data and has not said whether any delivered software is affected

SAP told BleepingComputer and dpa that it identified suspicious activity, promptly took the necessary measures to protect its customers, and found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data on the investigation to date; it gave no vector, actor, discovery date or list of affected systems (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-27; tagesschau.de, 2026-11-27; Handelsblatt, 2026-11-27). A letter that dpa saw in part places the activity within SAP's platform for developer productivity and software delivery on GitHub and asks staff to check whether they must change credentials (translated from German) (tagesschau.de, 2026-11-27). Handelsblatt, citing company circles, says SAP detected the incident the week before and that software development was attacked (translated from German) (Handelsblatt, 2026-11-27).

Reported by media from internal sources and not confirmed by SAP: DER SPIEGEL's insider says the attacker stole authentication tokens of SAP employees and used them to copy and also modify SAP source code on GitHub, and that the attackers may have had help from AI systems; heise, relaying Handelsblatt, reports that SAP restricted access to GitHub, stopped automated processes in software development and replaced signing keys; BleepingComputer, Handelsblatt and heise add that, according to SPIEGEL, SAP tracks the incident internally as Project Granite, a name SAP has not confirmed (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-27; DER SPIEGEL, 2026-11-26; heise online, 2026-11-27; Handelsblatt, 2026-11-27). SecurityWeek notes that none of the reports indicate tampered code reached software delivered to SAP customers, and WirtschaftsWoche that SAP has left open whether customers must act (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-27; WirtschaftsWoche, 2026-11-27). SAP is part of the Swiss public sector's estate: the Federal Audit Office says the federal administration runs SAP R/3, supported until the end of 2027 and being replaced with S/4HANA, and Inside IT reports an existing S/4HANA landscape in the canton of Zurich's administration; no Swiss impact is reported (EFK, 2023-05-10; Inside IT, 2026-11-27).

Exposure
Organisations that consume SAP-delivered code, packages or updates, or verify SAP signatures; SAP has said nothing on which artifacts or keys are in scope, and no source says delivered software is affected (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-27).
Detection
The reported behaviour is use of stolen employee tokens against a source-control platform; for SAP customers the observable is on their side of the boundary, namely the provenance of SAP-delivered artifacts and any signing-key change in SAP's own communications.
Defender takeaway
SAP customers should watch SAP's own security communications for which artifacts or signing keys are in scope and verify any key change through SAP's channel; no customer action has been published, and SAP declined to say whether customers pulling SAP code from GitHub should act (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-27). For your own pipelines, 1Password disclosed on 2026-11-25 an intrusion through an employee's corporate GitHub account (1Password, 2026-11-25); review how employee tokens reach source control and CI.

Builds on: 1Password breach via an employee GitHub account exported customer records; vaults not affected

item.title: Kudelski: assessed AI-driven insurer intrusion via onboarding and identity logic, no malware; alert on request bursts
item.description: Kudelski Security's incident responders describe a one-night intrusion at an unnamed European insurer in which about three million identification requests in under nine hours identified about 30 customers, more than a dozen accounts were created in customers' names without their passwords and more than 100 documents were extracted, with no malware and no compromise of the portal's servers. Kudelski assesses with high confidence that an offensive AI framework was used, names none and publishes no indicators, and traces the chain to business-logic weaknesses: the API of a retired web interface that stayed accessible, CAPTCHA and rate limits that were not enforced or were inactive after a migration, registration paths that did not consistently enforce prior identity checks, unverified contact data that inherited verified status, incomplete token validation and an identity-provider flaw in authenticator enrollment.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Kudelski Security: a one-night intrusion at a European insurer, assessed as run by an offensive AI framework, abused customer onboarding, identity migration and a retired API to create accounts in customers' names and extract more than 100 documents, with no malware

Kudelski Security's incident-response team describes a one-night intrusion at an unnamed European insurer in which about three million identification requests arrived in under nine hours, about 30 legitimate customer identities were identified, more than a dozen customer accounts were created in those customers' names without their passwords, and more than 100 documents with sensitive customer data were extracted (Kudelski Security, 2026-11-27). Kudelski found no malware and no compromise of the servers hosting the customer portal, and each forged account could read only its own customer's data (Kudelski Security, 2026-11-27). It assesses with high confidence that an offensive AI framework was used, from correlated indicators of compromise, infrastructure characteristics, previously documented attack patterns, machine-speed execution, application-specific reconnaissance and automated handling of complex identity workflows, names no framework and could not establish how much human supervision there was (Kudelski Security, 2026-11-27).

Among the weaknesses it lists, mostly business logic rather than software bugs: the API of a retired web interface remained accessible, identity information could be tested at scale, CAPTCHA was not enforced by the underlying API, rate limits were inactive after an infrastructure migration, alternative registration processes that did not consistently enforce prior identity checks, unverified contact information inherited a verified status, token validation was incomplete, authorization-related information was exposed to the client, and an identity-provider vulnerability weakened authenticator enrollment (Kudelski Security, 2026-11-27). The identity-provider flaw is cited as GHSA-qqv8-37gw-ww2q, which is ZITADEL's advisory for a missing second-factor check on authenticator enrollment in its Login V2 interface, affecting 4.0.0 through 4.20.4 and fixed in 4.20.5; the post does not say the insurer ran ZITADEL (ZITADEL, 2026-11-18). Kudelski compares the case with BabidiGhost: that operation tried an AI agent against many organizations, this one explored a single organization's interconnected application and identity ecosystem in depth (Kudelski Security, 2026-11-27).

Exposure
A customer or citizen portal that runs identity onboarding, identity migration or account recovery; the case came from an insurer, and the post names no public-sector victim.
Detection
Application and identity telemetry carried the evidence, not endpoint telemetry: Kudelski says abnormal application request volumes, extensive authentication failures and suspicious reconnaissance appeared well before data collection began and the attack still ran through the night (Kudelski Security, 2026-11-27). Its recommended detections include distributed requests against one business function across rotating infrastructure, excessive one-time-code failures, authenticator enrollment without completed MFA, activity against retired APIs, source-map access by automated clients and abnormal onboarding and recovery sequences (Kudelski Security, 2026-11-27). The sequence to alert on is a burst of identification requests, then accounts created in the names of existing customers without their original passwords, then sensitive information accessed by those accounts.

Triage: a newly created account may satisfy the portal's registration requirements, so a single account can look legitimate; Kudelski says abnormal request volumes, extensive authentication failures and reconnaissance activity were detectable well before data collection (Kudelski Security, 2026-11-27).

Defender takeaway
For any portal with identity lifecycle workflows, Kudelski's hardening list is the checklist: user-supplied contact attributes must not inherit verified status, identity migrations must preserve existing account activation states, retiring a front end includes decommissioning its supporting APIs, and rate limiting, CAPTCHA and server-side validation must be tested again after each change (Kudelski Security, 2026-11-27); alert on identification-request bursts, and move a ZITADEL deployment on 4.0.0 through 4.20.4 to 4.20.5 (ZITADEL, 2026-11-18).

Builds on: BabidiGhost AI agent targeted 50+ organisations, mostly in Belgium, France, Switzerland; MFA…

item.title: Hunt.io: crew staged a Swiss tax office's AD database via ntdsutil IFM; fake JDBC driver loader; edge exploit kit
item.description: Hunt.io recovered three exposed attacker directories and reports a domain-controller workflow against "a Swiss tax office": a log of ntdsutil install-from-media creation and a script that copies the Active Directory database and registry hives from a controller share to staging, decodes them and requests removal of the media. Complete off-host transfer is not confirmed, the victim is unnamed and the report does not show how access was gained. The kit also holds a Java loader registered as a Microsoft SQL Server JDBC driver, Apollo- and Poseidon-derived implants, a commercial employee-monitoring product used as a command channel and staged exploits for edge services that Hunt.io says show availability, not success; it assesses a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking, Southeast Asia-based crew and names no group.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB3

Hunt.io: exposed attacker directories show a crew staging a Swiss tax office's domain-controller database through ntdsutil install-from-media, a Java loader posing as the SQL Server JDBC driver and an exploit kit for edge services; the Swiss victim is unnamed, the access route is not shown and complete transfer is unconfirmed

Hunt.io recovered the contents of three exposed open directories and, reading the operators' own files, reports a domain-controller workflow against a Swiss tax office: a log records ntdsutil install-from-media creation, and a script copies the domain database and the registry hives from a controller share to a staging area, decodes them with a single-byte XOR and then requests removal of the install-from-media set (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25). Hunt.io says complete off-host transfer is not independently confirmed, that an NTLM-relay run against an internal LDAP service belongs to the same environment, and that the Swiss output begins after code execution was already available, so how the crew first got in is not shown (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25). The report names no canton, commune or federal body, and Hunt.io says it notified CISA before publishing (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25).

The same files hold a Java class registered as a java.sql.Driver service provider that poses as Microsoft's SQL Server JDBC driver: its boot routine runs when an application loads the JAR, with no scheduled task needed, and either polls an HTTPS endpoint on TCP 8443 for commands passed to cmd.exe or decodes a packed file into an Apollo-derived Windows executable written under the Java temp directory and started from Java (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25). Hunt.io also describes a Poseidon-derived Linux implant behind a server labelled Mythic, a commercial employee-monitoring product whose agents the operators drive with custom clients, and a reconnaissance stage that sends base64-encoded output in chunks inside GET request paths; it says the artifacts show a Poseidon-derived build, which does not establish that it ran on an external victim, and an Apollo derivation with no verified runtime command-and-control configuration (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25). Staged exploits cover edge and remote-access services, among them Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2025-5777), FreePBX (CVE-2025-57819) and PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), and Hunt.io states that their presence establishes availability, not successful operation against any named target (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25). Hunt.io reads the operation as a Chinese-speaking, Southeast Asia-based cybercrime crew running a Russian-authored toolkit and ties it to no named group and no state sponsor (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
Active Directory domain controllers and Java application servers that load third-party JARs; Hunt.io's other victims are a US hospital system, a US manufacturer and a Bangladeshi university; law firms and US federal agencies are mainly reconnaissance targets, and one law firm was attacked without success (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25).
Detection
On domain controllers, ntdsutil install-from-media creation that no administrator requested, followed by reads of the database and the SYSTEM and SECURITY hive copies from the share by another host and a removal of the media; NTLM relay and coercion activity against domain controllers; on Java application servers, a JAR whose service-provider descriptor names a com.microsoft.sqlserver.jdbc class that matches no vendor build, java writing an executable under the temp directory and then starting a child process, and HTTPS polling from application servers to TCP 8443; in proxy logs, GET paths carrying long base64 chunks (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25).
Defender takeaway
Hunt domain controllers for install-from-media creation and share-staged copies of the directory database and hives, and enforce SMB signing and LDAP channel binding, which Hunt.io names as the hardening against the relay and coercion tooling; review Java servers for unexpected JDBC providers, and treat the Swiss victim claim as a single-source reading of recovered files until a Swiss body or the victim comments.

item.title: RealVNC CVE-2026-137738: pre-auth UDP flaw can run code, as root on some platforms; update Server to 7.19.1
item.description: RealVNC's advisory RVNC-2026-001 of 2026-11-20 fixes CVE-2026-137738 (CVSS 3.1 9.8), a memory-safety flaw in UDP-based connections that can be exploited before authentication to run code remotely, as root on certain platforms, or to crash the software; it affects cloud-hosted connectivity and manually configured direct connections, and TCP-only direct connections are not exposed. Fixed builds are Server 7.19.1, Viewer 8.6.2, Connect App 8.6.2, Classic Viewer 7.18.3 and On-Demand Assist 3.5.0 with matching mobile releases; RealVNC knows of no exploitation, and ENISA's entry followed on 2026-11-27.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-137738NATOA2

CVE-2026-137738, RealVNC Server 6.4.0 to 7.19.0 and the Viewer, Connect App and On-Demand Assist builds: a pre-authentication memory-safety flaw in UDP-based connections can give remote code execution, as root on certain platforms; fixed in Server 7.19.1, TCP-only direct connections are not exposed, no exploitation reported (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

RealVNC's advisory RVNC-2026-001 of 2026-11-20 fixes CVE-2026-137738, rated Critical with CVSS 3.1 9.8: a memory-safety flaw in UDP-based connections that could potentially be exploited before authentication to execute code remotely or crash the software, and that could give an attacker remote code execution as root on certain platforms (RealVNC, 2026-11-20; ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-27). RealVNC says it affects all customers using its cloud-hosted connectivity and manually configured direct connections, offline-licensed and on-premises deployments included, and that TCP-only direct connections are not exposed (RealVNC, 2026-11-20). ENISA's entry appeared on 2026-11-27 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-27), the day heise reported the flaw (heise online, 2026-11-27).

Affected are Server 6.4.0 to 7.19.0, Viewer 8.4.0 to 8.6.1, Classic Viewer 6.4.0 to 7.18.2, Connect App 8.6.1 and earlier, On-Demand Assist 3.4.1 and earlier, the iOS and iPadOS Viewer 3.7.0 to 4.9.5, the Android Viewer 3.5.0 to 4.9.5, iOS Server 2.8.1 and earlier and Android Server 2.8.3 and earlier; the fixed builds are Server 7.19.1, Viewer 8.6.2, Connect App 8.6.2, Classic Viewer 7.18.3, On-Demand Assist 3.5.0, the iOS and iPadOS and Android Viewers 4.9.6, iOS and iPadOS Server 2.8.2 and Android Server 2.8.4 (RealVNC, 2026-11-20). Updating is the only remedy RealVNC names, and for On-Demand Assist it tells administrators to advise end users to delete copies of older versions that they downloaded earlier (RealVNC, 2026-11-20). RealVNC says it is not aware of active exploitation in the wild, and heise repeats that no attacks are known (translated from German) (RealVNC, 2026-11-20; heise online, 2026-11-27).

Exposure
RealVNC Server, Viewer, Classic Viewer, Connect App or On-Demand Assist at the builds above that is reached through RealVNC's cloud connectivity or a manually configured direct connection; a server that accepts only TCP direct connections is not exposed (RealVNC, 2026-11-20). The advisory names no UDP port and does not say which platforms run the service as root.
Detection
Crashes or restarts of the RealVNC Server service and, on hosts where it runs as root, unexpected child processes of that service; both follow from the pre-authentication memory-corruption mechanism the vendor describes, which publishes no indicator; in network telemetry, unexpected inbound UDP to hosts that run the server is the pivot, since the flaw sits in UDP-based connections.
Defender takeaway
Inventory every RealVNC component, including On-Demand Assist copies that users downloaded, and update to the fixed builds, hosts reachable by direct connections or cloud connectivity first; RealVNC names no workaround, so the update is the control, and no exploitation is known.

item.title: FreeRADIUS 3.2.11, 3.0.29: Critical unauthenticated use-after-free in default EAP-TTLS, TEAP bypasses; upgrade
item.description: FreeRADIUS announced 3.0.29 and 3.2.11 on 2026-11-25; the project's page lists 21 fixed issues, one rated Critical: an unauthenticated use-after-free in the EAP-TTLS module, which is enabled in the default configuration and where code execution may be possible. Eight issues rated High sit mostly in modules the project says are off by default, and three Medium TEAP issues let an unauthenticated peer obtain an Access-Accept on 3.2.x; the project states no exploitation and no proof of concept for the Critical flaw. CERT-FR restated the release on 2026-11-27, and 3.0.29 is planned as the last 3.0 release.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOA2

FreeRADIUS before 3.0.29 and 3.2.11: a Critical use-after-free in the default-enabled EAP-TTLS module can be started by an unauthenticated user and code execution may be possible; 21 issues fixed in all, among them TEAP bugs that return Access-Accept to an unauthenticated peer; no exploitation stated and no proof of concept for the Critical flaw

FreeRADIUS announced 3.0.29 and 3.2.11 on its security page of 2026-11-25 (GitHub release pages: 2026-11-26), fixing various overflows and memory leaks, and recommends that everyone on earlier versions upgrade (FreeRADIUS, 2026-11-25). The page lists 21 issues: one Critical, eight High, five Medium and seven Low (FreeRADIUS, 2026-11-25). The Critical issue is a use-after-free in the TTLS module, which the project says is enabled in the default configuration: an unauthenticated user could start an EAP-TTLS session and send invalid inner-tunnel data, and with heap shaping an attacker can cause a write of a heap pointer to a chosen address, so code execution may be possible (FreeRADIUS, 2026-11-25). The page states no exploitation and no proof of concept for this flaw, mentions a proof of concept that Ada Logics wrote for two High EAP-FAST issues, and says a system whose affected module is not enabled is not vulnerable to that module's issues (FreeRADIUS, 2026-11-25).

The High issues in DHCP, EAP-FAST, EAP-SIM and TEAP are in modules the project says are not enabled by default, among them an unauthenticated out-of-bounds write in the DHCP option encoder (FreeRADIUS, 2026-11-25). Three Medium TEAP issues let an unauthenticated peer that starts a TEAP session obtain an Access-Accept, through skipped Basic-Password checks, a Crypto-Binding check missing in production builds and an unexpected Crypto-Binding TLV; their fixes are listed on 3.2.x only, and TEAP is off by default (FreeRADIUS, 2026-11-25). CERT-FR restated the release on 2026-11-27, saying some of the flaws allow remote code execution, remote denial of service and a breach of data confidentiality (translated from French) (CERT-FR, 2026-11-27). The project page lists no CVE ids; ENISA's database lists CVE-2026-127030, an EAP-FAST session-ticket stack overflow, and CVE-2026-127029, an EAP-SIM identity-length stack overflow, both published on 2026-11-12 and scored CVSS 3.1 7.5 for availability impact only (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-12; ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
FreeRADIUS before 3.0.29 or 3.2.11 with the TTLS module enabled, as it is in the default configuration, for the Critical flaw; the project says EAP-TLS, TTLS and PEAP are enabled by default, and it states no default for the EAP-MSCHAPv2 module of a High issue, which a PEAP-only site should check; the issues in TEAP, EAP-FAST, EAP-SIM and DHCP apply only where those modules are enabled (FreeRADIUS, 2026-11-25). The project's standing advice on the same page, from its earlier 2026-06-01 announcement, is to keep the RADIUS server on a management VLAN and off the internet (FreeRADIUS, 2026-11-25).
Detection
Radiusd crashes and restarts, as service-manager events or core dumps, that follow EAP-TTLS handshakes, and on servers with TEAP enabled, Access-Accept replies for TEAP sessions with no completed inner authentication in the authentication detail log; both follow from the mechanisms the project describes, which publishes no indicator. A heap-corruption attack may leave only a crash, so review radiusd restarts in the days before the upgrade.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 3.2.11, or to 3.0.29 on a 3.0 server and then migrate, because the release notes call 3.0.29 the planned last 3.0 release and tell everyone to move to 3.2.11 or later (FreeRADIUS 3.0.29, 2026-11-26); check which EAP methods the server enables and switch off those in use by nobody, and keep the listener reachable only from network access servers and proxies. The Critical flaw sits in a method that is on by default, though no exploitation is stated.

item.title: Cacti 1.2.31 zero-day 4HTTP2ROOT: guest-session RCE, public PoC, no release; disable the guest user, restrict the UI
item.description: A researcher published a proof of concept on 2026-11-26 that takes Cacti Core 1.2.31 from an anonymous guest session to command execution as the web or poller account in four requests; no CVE id and no release exist, and the chain needs the guest account enabled, which Cacti's documentation says is off by default. Previdian's honeypots recorded SQL-injection attempts from 2026-11-27 with no confirmed success, and Cacti merged unreleased hardening commits on 2026-11-28 that cover each stage without referring to the disclosure. Cacti stores SNMP strings and device logins, so a compromised server is a pivot into the monitored network.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Cacti Core 1.2.31 (4HTTP2ROOT): an anonymous guest session reaches a stored SQL injection and command execution as the web or poller account in four requests, public proof of concept, no CVE id and no release; the chain needs the guest account enabled, which Cacti's documentation says is off by default

A researcher using the handle ek0ms savi0r published a write-up and proof of concept on 2026-11-26 for unauthenticated command execution on Cacti Core 1.2.31 in four HTTP requests that start from an anonymous guest session, a chain its repository calls 4HTTP2SHELL (ek0ms savi0r, 2026-11-26) and watchTowr named 4HTTP2ROOT (watchTowr, 2026-11-26). BleepingComputer relays the researcher's statement that the flaw was not reported to Cacti before release, and no fixed version exists: watchTowr says Cacti has not published one, and the project's releases page lists 1.2.31 as its newest release on 2026-11-28 (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-27; watchTowr, 2026-11-26; Cacti releases, 2026-11-28).

As RavenAI and The Hacker News describe the chain, the guest profile page stores a non-numeric graph page size; a graph-preview request concatenates it into a query that accepts a second statement, which rewrites a poller entry's command; and a realtime-graph request runs that command inside the web request as the web server and poller account, often a low-privileged web user according to watchTowr (RavenAI, 2026-11-26; The Hacker News, 2026-11-27; watchTowr, 2026-11-26). The guest account must be enabled for the chain to work, and Cacti's documentation says guest or anonymous access is disabled by default and works only when the Guest user is enabled and set as the guest user (watchTowr, 2026-11-26; Cacti documentation, 2026-11-28). Only 1.2.31 was tested, and it is unclear whether earlier versions are affected (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-27). Cacti stores SNMP strings and device logins, so a compromised server is a foothold into the monitored network (watchTowr, 2026-11-26).

watchTowr reports no exploitation as of 2026-11-27, while Previdian's honeypots recorded SQL-injection attempts from 2026-11-27 that it says do not show the target was vulnerable or that an attempt succeeded (watchTowr, 2026-11-26; Previdian, 2026-11-26; Previdian tracker, 2026-11-26). BSI classifies the issue as critical (BSI, 2026-11-26). On 2026-11-28 the project merged unreleased 1.2.x hardening commits that reject guest profile writes, validate the page size and require graph access before a realtime command, without referring to the disclosure and with no release or advisory yet (Cacti pull request 9014, 2026-11-28).

Exposure
Cacti Core 1.2.31 with the Guest user enabled and set as the anonymous user, reachable from wherever an attacker can load the web interface.
Detection
In web access logs, one client requesting the guest profile page, a profile update, a graph preview and a realtime graph in sequence; in the application log, a PHP warning about a non-numeric value in a graph display setting; in the Cacti database, a poller entry whose command is anything other than a normal poller command; on the host, new files written by the poller or web account, a shell or marker file among them (RavenAI, 2026-11-26; watchTowr, 2026-11-26). No release exists, so check guest-reachable servers for these artifacts and treat stored SNMP strings and device logins as exposed on a hit.

Triage: each request alone is ordinary guest behavior, so the stronger pivots are the non-numeric display-setting warning and a changed poller entry followed by a realtime-graph request (RavenAI, 2026-11-26).

Defender takeaway
Where the guest account is on, disable it and restrict the web interface to trusted internal networks now and review poller entries for unexpected commands; where it is off, the sources say the chain has no entry point, but watch for the first release with the hardening commits (watchTowr, 2026-11-26).

item.title: Update: Puppet Enterprise report-deserialization RCE is on CISA KEV; upgrade to 2023.8.13, 2025.12.1 or 2026.0.1
item.description: Huntback's decoy captured the exploit chain for CVE-2026-115731 on 2026-11-19, two days after the KEV listing: a certificate request, a fetch of the signed certificate that tests for autosigning, and a report upload carrying a type definition, which it reads as a check for vulnerable servers. The hunt signal is a PUT to the certificate-request path from a non-agent address, a GET for the same name within seconds, then a PUT to the report path.
item.content:encoded:
Update27 Nov 2026 04:58 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsourcing_notesourcesevidenceactionsbodyupdated_at

Huntback's decoy captured the exploit chain for CVE-2026-115731 on 2026-11-19, two days after the KEV listing: a certificate request, a fetch of the signed certificate that tests for autosigning, and a report upload carrying a type definition, which it reads as a check for vulnerable servers. The hunt signal is a PUT to the certificate-request path from a non-agent address, a GET for the same name within seconds, then a PUT to the report path.

Huntback, a research firm that runs decoy servers, captured the whole exploit chain on one Puppet Server decoy on the morning of 2026-11-19, in 1.47 seconds from one address (Huntback, 2026-11-20). The chain is a bare certificate request for a generated node name, which a CA that asks for a shared secret or other proof would refuse, a fetch of the signed certificate 1.4 seconds later without polling, which answers 200 only where the CA signs automatically, and a report upload whose wrapper is ordinary and whose event carries a type definition with a Ruby method annotation (Huntback, 2026-11-20). Huntback reads it as a check for vulnerable servers: the decoy signed the certificate, accepted the report with a 200 and returned no marker, and the same address had tried exploits for four other products in the previous ten days (Huntback, 2026-11-20). A scout from a different address had probed the status service and the CA paths about two and a half hours earlier without asking for a certificate. Huntback's advice is to list the signed certificates (puppetserver ca list --all) and account for every name, to refuse at a reverse proxy any report containing RubyMethod, since no agent sends a type definition in a report, and to keep TCP 8140 closed to networks that are not agents'; none of this is vendor guidance (Huntback, 2026-11-20). The capture is a single source and Huntback names no actor or victim.

Open finding: CVE-2026-115731, Puppet Enterprise before 2023.8.13, 2025.12.1 and 2026.0.1: deserialization of a crafted agent report gives code execution as the Puppet service user to any holder of a CA-signed agent certificate, and unauthenticated where the CA autosigns; CISA lists it as exploited (CVSS 4.0 9.4) →

item.title: Update: Zammad 6.5.5 emergency-fixes the exploited session-leak RCE on 6.5; 7.2.3 now supersedes 7.2.2 (root escalation)
item.description: DIVD's forensic report of 2026-11-25 says the attacker likely used ARTEX and moved from the Zammad host to Jira and Confluence by ARP poisoning an unencrypted database link and forging administrator session tokens, took credentials from Zammad's database, and kept cloud OAuth access after network isolation. The alert fired 7 h 21 min before a volunteer looked at it and 19 h 23 min before the CISO was informed; containment finished 27 h 41 min after it.
item.content:encoded:
Update27 Nov 2026 04:56 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsummaryentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

DIVD's forensic report of 2026-11-25 says the attacker likely used ARTEX and moved from the Zammad host to Jira and Confluence by ARP poisoning an unencrypted database link and forging administrator session tokens, took credentials from Zammad's database, and kept cloud OAuth access after network isolation. The alert fired 7 h 21 min before a volunteer looked at it and 19 h 23 min before the CISO was informed; containment finished 27 h 41 min after it.

DIVD published the forensic report on its September breach on 2026-11-25 (DIVD CSIRT blog, 2026-11-25), written by Merlon Security with NVISO's analysis of the Google Workspace side. It says the attacker likely used ARTEX, on the basis of 990 scripts and 3,259 output files, scripts commented in an LLM style, an API token named artex- plus a number and a Zammad administrator account named artex.ops, ARTEX strings in an e-mail subject and the numeric job IDs that ARTEX's intents use; it names no actor (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

The chain at behaviour level: the attacker probed the perimeter from 07:40 UTC on 2026-09-21; an administrator logged in to Zammad at 18:53 and the WebSocket flaw yielded that session cookie 1.3 seconds later; the replayed session wrote a file through the package-upload endpoint at 19:06 and a malicious Ruby mail template as an override of a mailer view at 19:27, which a user-creation request rendered, giving code execution as the zammad user at 19:27:58. Command and control ran through a Zammad API endpoint, with files staged in the web-served directory and fetched back through the egress proxy because direct outbound traffic was blocked. Root followed through the second flaw: a service that runs as root read configuration from a directory the zammad account owned, and a dropped file plus a kill of the web worker, which the supervisor restarted, gave root by 19:46 and left a setuid copy of bash (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

From the Zammad host, in the same web-application VLAN as Jira and Confluence, the attacker sniffed passively from 21:19 and from about 01:37 on 2026-09-22 ran ARP-poisoning scripts, reaching a man-in-the-middle position between Confluence and its PostgreSQL database at 02:27. The link was unencrypted, so it read the database protocol, learned the schema from captured traffic and injected its own SQL into live connections, writing a remember-me session token of its choosing for an administrator into Confluence's token table and presenting it at 08:49; Jira followed through its OAuth tables and a replay of remember-me tokens at 14:08. The report says TLS on the database links would have stopped the injection, asks for deny-by-default micro-segmentation inside the VLAN and says a containerised Zammad would have prevented the root step (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Persistence was a new Zammad administrator account and API tokens, a root-run systemd loop with Restart=always and cron entries that run text files dropped in the web-served directory, and an edit of Zammad's Google sign-in initializer that switched the access type to offline and added the Gmail scope, which captured nothing because no user signed in while it was live. Credentials taken included the hosting provider's mailbox password in cleartext, OAuth tokens for the two shared mailboxes, the database password, an Elastic credential and Jira's OAuth consumer private key and password hashes. NVISO says the content of the two shared mailboxes up to the credential and session resets must be considered potentially compromised, and that tokens were re-issued after the network isolation, so network isolation alone does not revoke cloud OAuth access (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

The alert fired at 19:43 UTC on 2026-09-21. A volunteer first looked at it at 03:04 on 09-22, 7 h 21 min later; the CISO was informed at 15:06, 19 h 23 min after the alert; and isolation completed at 23:24, 27 h 41 min after it (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Contradiction: DIVD's case page says "it took us 19 hours to initiate our first response on 22 September 2026" (DIVD, 2026-11-25), while the report says "The first response to these alerts was observed on Sep 22nd 2026 at 03:04 UTC", 7 h 21 min after the alert, and puts the CISO notification at 15:06 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24). The case page's own metrics table lists a mean time to acknowledge of 07:20:51 ("Time between first alert and SOC pickup") and a mean time to respond of 19:16:51 ("Time between first attack and formal response"), the same 7 h 21 min the report gives for the first look and about the 19 hours of the prose, so the two documents use "first response" for different intervals (DIVD, 2026-11-25). The report counts about 39 hours of actor interaction in the cloud, to 08:33 on 2026-09-23 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Open finding: CVE-2026-102489 / CVE-2026-102490, Zammad helpdesk: a session-hijack remote code execution and a zammad-to-root escalation, both reported exploited since 21 September; 7.2.2 fixes the root flaw on DEB and RPM installs →

Update27 Nov 2026 04:55 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelheadlinesummaryaffected_productsentitiescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

nginx 1.31.10 and 1.30.8 (2026-11-23) and NGINX Plus 37.3.1.1 and 37.0.9.1 fix a further flaw, CPU exhaustion when ssl_early_data is on (CVE-2026-132779), so the update target moves; Veeam lists its 13.1 Software and Infrastructure Appliances as affected by the two HTTP/2 flaws with a fix through Veeam Updater since 2026-11-25, and GitLab's Linux package carries nginx 1.31.9.

nginx 1.31.10 and 1.30.8, both dated 2026-11-23, carry one security fix: when ssl_early_data is configured a client might cause excessive CPU usage (CVE-2026-132779) (nginx.org, 2026-11-23; nginx.org, 2026-11-23). nginx.org lists it as affecting 1.21.4 to 1.31.9 (nginx.org, 2026-11-27), so 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix the memory-corruption flaws but not this one; NGINX Plus 37.3.1.1 and 37.0.9.1 of the same day are security releases whose only fix is this flaw, and the 18 November Plus builds do not carry it (F5 NGINX Plus release notes, 2026-11-23). F5's own advisory and a score were not readable, and no source states whether R33 to R36 are affected.

Veeam's KB4976 lists Veeam Software Appliance 13.1 and Veeam Infrastructure Appliance 13.1 as affected by CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, because their nginx has HTTP/2 enabled on a listener that proxies requests to a backend; the other three flaws do not apply (Veeam, 2026-11-25). A fix has been in the Veeam repository since 2026-11-25, Veeam Updater checks every 12 hours and installs mandatory updates automatically on the nearest Sunday at 14:00, and until it is installed Veeam says to restrict TCP 443 on the appliances to trusted networks, because HTTP/2 cannot be disabled on them (Veeam, 2026-11-25). GitLab's Linux package and Docker images carry nginx 1.31.9 from 19.6.2, 19.5.9 and 19.4.11, and its page does not say whether they set ssl_early_data (GitLab, 2026-11-25). KB4976 also lists the Veeam Plug-In for AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure appliances as affected (install all available security updates through Veeam Updater) and Veeam Backup for Salesforce 3.2.1, which is affected by the same two HTTP/2 flaws (install the operating system vendor's update or disable HTTP/2); Veeam manages its Data Cloud services and asks for no customer action (Veeam, 2026-11-25).

item.title: Update: FBI: various actors run ARTEX against many sectors, government included; Microsoft now names six users
item.description: Wiz shows that ARTEX writes a numeric intent ID from a per-installation counter it does not reset by default, and Cairn a per-project one, into AWS and Azure resource names, session names and comments, a pivot for hunting and linking activity; Wiz ties ARTEX-Harvester to more than a dozen organisations, Huntback's exposed console shows a Global Administrator takeover at a South Korean university, and DIVD's forensic report finds the same numbering in its own breach.
item.content:encoded:
Update27 Nov 2026 04:54 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsummaryentitiessourcesevidencesourcing_notebodyupdated_at

Wiz shows that ARTEX writes a numeric intent ID from a per-installation counter it does not reset by default, and Cairn a per-project one, into AWS and Azure resource names, session names and comments, a pivot for hunting and linking activity; Wiz ties ARTEX-Harvester to more than a dozen organisations, Huntback's exposed console shows a Global Administrator takeover at a South Korean university, and DIVD's forensic report finds the same numbering in its own breach.

Wiz Research shows how ARTEX and Cairn leak their intent numbering into victim logs. ARTEX draws intents, facts, findings, hints and digests from one counter per installation that is never reset by default, so intent numbers climb across runs and targets and consecutive ones are rare, and it puts the number in its working directory, its session name and its prompt; Cairn formats zero-padded counters per object type and resets them for every project (Wiz, 2026-11-25). The numbers surface wherever an API takes a name or comment: AWS role session names, SSM command comments, KMS key descriptions and aliases, security-group rule descriptions, Azure run-command, VM and app-registration names, and the error message of a denied call (Wiz, 2026-11-25). Wiz uses them to link activity across rotating residential-proxy addresses and victims, to separate installations and to read scope from a jump far larger than the activity in one victim's logs, and cautions that hits are tool markers and pacing clues, not operator fingerprints: unrelated installations collide in the same ranges and operators reset or parallelise (Wiz, 2026-11-25). Google's report of 2026-10-31 had already seen incremental numeric markers in ARTEX file names, account names, passwords and e-mail subjects without being able to explain them (GTIG and Mandiant, 2026-10-31).

Wiz's account of ARTEX-Harvester ties it, at varying confidence, to activity at more than a dozen organisations between late October and mid-November, clustered by a distinctive boto3 build, the cross-victim intent counter and proxy-pool overlap, and warns that activity labelled ARTEX comes from multiple unrelated operators; these two posts do not mention Storm-0940 (Wiz, 2026-11-23).

Huntback reads an exposed ARTEX console whose workspace holds a South Korean university, where the numbering also leaks onto the victim, with a local administrator account named after an intent number. Single sign-on accepted a stored password hash as the password, a Microsoft 365 password-reset bridge ignored the old password, and a password-grant token, which involves no browser and no second factor, carried Global Administrator from 18:47:53 UTC on 2026-11-16; student-style accounts were then created and licensed and a further account was made Global Administrator (Huntback, 2026-11-24). Huntback says a Conditional Access policy requiring multi-factor authentication for every user and blocking legacy and non-interactive password sign-ins would have stopped the token request, names no actor, and says its detection queries were not run against a live workspace (Huntback, 2026-11-24).

DIVD's forensic report on its own September breach says the attacker was likely using ARTEX and that ARTEX's intents are numeric job IDs included in all input and output (DIVD, 2026-11-24).

Open finding: ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration →

item.title: Update: PAN-OS management interfaces rooted via PHP2Shell and a kernel flaw, both exploited per Palo Alto: hotfix, then check
item.description: Palo Alto's bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015 (2026-11-24, labelled Informational) says exploitation of the kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 has been observed against internet-exposed management interfaces, which makes the vendor itself a source for the second half of the chain Dream Research described, and lists a later hotfix in every train that fixes the kernel flaw as well as the PHP flaws.
item.content:encoded:
Update27 Nov 2026 04:53 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelheadlinesummaryupdated_atcvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Palo Alto's bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015 (2026-11-24, labelled Informational) says exploitation of the kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 has been observed against internet-exposed management interfaces, which makes the vendor itself a source for the second half of the chain Dream Research described, and lists a later hotfix in every train that fixes the kernel flaw as well as the PHP flaws.

Palo Alto Networks published bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015 on 2026-11-24 at 23:10 UTC (its timeline's initial-publication entry; the page header reads 2026-11-25), titled "OSS CVEs Fixed in PAN-OS" and labelled Informational with a zero CVSS block; its exploitation-status block reads "Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet" (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24). CVE-2026-46300 is the Linux kernel flaw Dream Research chained with PHP2Shell, so the vendor now itself states exploitation of the second half of the chain that Dream Research described; CISA's catalog has listed the kernel flaw as exploited since 2026-10-28 (CISA KEV, 2026-11-25). The bulletin's FAQ says all observed exploitation targeted devices with an internet-exposed management interface, that a device on a fixed PAN-OS listed in the PHP2Shell advisory is protected, and that "The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability through an internet-exposed management interface, and we are not aware of any other exploitation method"; it still recommends upgrading to a fixed release at the next maintenance interval where management access is restricted, and upgrading immediately and restricting access where the management interface or a dataplane interface with a management profile is internet-reachable (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24).

The bulletin lists the first fixed build for the kernel flaw per train, two to four hotfixes after the PHP2Shell build: 12.2.4-h3; 12.1.4-h15, 12.1.7-h15, 12.1.10-h6; 11.2.4-h25, 11.2.7-h25, 11.2.10-h19, 11.2.13-h6, 11.2.16-h3; 11.1.4-h40, 11.1.6-h42, 11.1.7-h14, 11.1.10-h38, 11.1.13-h18, 11.1.16-h6; 10.2.7-h41, 10.2.10-h45, 10.2.13-h29, 10.2.16-h14, 10.2.18-h15. It has no workaround section and no affected-product table and says nothing on Panorama, Prisma Access or Cloud NGFW for this flaw; its mitigation is restricting management access to trusted internal addresses (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24).

Open finding: CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Panorama: the PHP2Shell flaws affect every release below its train's hotfix through the management web interface, and Palo Alto reports active exploitation against internet-exposed management interfaces; all twenty hotfixes are out →

item.title: Update: Mitel MiCollab AWV flaws exploited pre-advisory per Accenture APEX, CISA lists them; patching alone does not evict
item.description: Accenture APEX Labs reports that the AWV flaws were exploited before Mitel's advisory and patch: web-shell activity at one victim before 23:00 UTC on 2026-11-15, root within about 30 minutes, directory credentials recovered from MiCollab's LDAP configuration and used against a domain controller, local logs edited, and a second organisation's server talking to the same actor since 2026-11-09. A patched server cannot be assumed clean.
item.content:encoded:
Update27 Nov 2026 04:52 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

Accenture APEX Labs reports that the AWV flaws were exploited before Mitel's advisory and patch: web-shell activity at one victim before 23:00 UTC on 2026-11-15, root within about 30 minutes, directory credentials recovered from MiCollab's LDAP configuration and used against a domain controller, local logs edited, and a second organisation's server talking to the same actor since 2026-11-09. A patched server cannot be assumed clean.

Accenture APEX Labs reports that the MISA-2026-0012 flaws were exploited before Mitel published its advisory and patch. At one victim organisation it places web-shell activity before 23:00 UTC on 2026-11-15, with high confidence, when it was still 15 November in every time zone from UTC−12 to UTC+1 and Mitel dated its advisory 16 November (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). Counted from the first observed request, the actor checked the version, bypassed authentication within a minute, had two uploads accepted at 9 minutes, ran its first web-shell command as the web service account at 12 minutes, reached root between 15 and 30 minutes with system logs reset as a side effect, and at 32 minutes used the credentials recovered from MiCollab's LDAP configuration to authenticate to a domain controller over LDAPS; it then filtered web-shell requests out of the local web, error and admin logs and, 20 to 23 hours in, dumped databases on a backup server and a database server and uploaded the archives over many short HTTPS sessions (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). APEX withholds how root was obtained and does not say which of the five flaws were used.

A second organisation's MiCollab server, on a 10.0-series release exposed to this advisory and to the July one, has held a persistent HTTPS channel to the same actor server since 2026-11-09, and APEX has not determined how it was compromised. APEX assesses that AI-assisted tooling operating on the actor's server drove parts of the intrusion, an inference from sampled traffic to two commercial AI API services that it says cannot show exactly how they were used, and it names no group (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). Mitel's advisory is unchanged at revision 2.0 and makes no exploitation statement; BSI's revision of 2026-11-25 rates it critical and says active exploitation was reported (BSI, 2026-11-25).

Open finding: Mitel MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier, MISA-2026-0012: an unauthenticated blind command injection in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing component (CVSS 3.1 10.0) and four more flaws there, one an XML injection that can run commands (9.0); CVE-2026-133323 and CVE-2026-133303 lead the five assigned CVE ids, patch KB000129195, Accenture APEX Labs reports exploitation before the advisory and CISA lists all five as exploited since 2026-11-25 →

item.title: NFS2ROOT: Linux nfsd pre-auth heap overflow, root shell claimed; limit TCP 2049, Ubuntu and RHEL 9/10 not fixed
item.description: CVE-2026-99362 is an unauthenticated heap overflow in the Linux kernel NFS server (nfsd) over NFSv4.1 or 4.2, scored CVSS 3.1 9.8 in the CVE record, that OpenSec says it turned into a root shell with one TCP connection to port 2049. It is fixed upstream in 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1 (later also 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193 and 6.6.163), but on 2026-11-27 Ubuntu and RHEL 9 and 10 list no fixed kernel; the exploit is private and no exploitation is reported.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-99362NATOB2

NFS2ROOT, CVE-2026-99362, Linux kernel NFS server (nfsd): an unauthenticated heap overflow over NFSv4.1 or 4.2 that OpenSec says it turned into a root shell with one TCP connection to port 2049 (CVSS 3.1 9.8); fixed upstream in 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1, Ubuntu and RHEL 9 and 10 list no fixed kernel on 2026-11-27, exploit private, no exploitation reported

CVE-2026-99362 is a heap out-of-bounds write in the Linux kernel's NFS server: nfsd4_sequence() narrows the reply buffer to the session's cached-reply limit before it accepts the slot sequence id, a client can negotiate that limit down so every slot has a zero-length buffer, and the server then caches a whole reply into a buffer with no room; the flaw has been present since Linux 3.16 (Linux kernel CVE team, 2026-11-19). The announcement lists fixes in 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1 (Linux kernel CVE team, 2026-11-19); ENISA's record, last updated on 2026-11-23, adds 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193 and 6.6.163 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-23).

OpenSec, which reported it, says an unauthenticated client reaches a root shell with one TCP connection to port 2049 over NFSv4.1 or 4.2, shows this in its own recording and says its exploit stays private (OpenSec, 2026-11-25). watchTowr reports no exploitation in the wild as of 2026-11-26 (watchTowr, 2026-11-26), and the fix with its root-cause text has been public on the linux-nfs list since 2026-08-17 (linux-nfs, 2026-08-17).

Distribution status as read on 2026-11-27: Debian trixie and the 6.12 backport kernel for bookworm are fixed, bookworm's default 6.1 kernel is not (Debian, 2026-11-27); Red Hat fixed RHEL 8 on 2026-11-26 (RHSA-2026:103817) while RHEL 9 and 10 are listed as affected with no fix (Red Hat, 2026-11-26); Ubuntu shows no fixed kernel on any release from 16.04 to 26.10 (Ubuntu, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
A host that serves NFS. Red Hat says default RHEL does not run nfsd, which limits the attack surface to systems configured to export NFSv4.1 or 4.2 shares (Red Hat, 2026-11-26). OpenSec's test is nfsd loaded, /proc/fs/nfsd/versions showing +4.1 or +4.2 and a listener on port 2049 on a non-loopback address, with a kernel older than the fixed one and no distribution backport (OpenSec, 2026-11-25). No source says whether an empty export list or client-address restrictions reduce the reach.
Detection
OpenSec says the traffic is valid NFS with no network signature and names kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, oopses with nfsd4, svc or call_usermodehelper frames, shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server and bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source; no vendor confirms these (OpenSec, 2026-11-25). On a server that was reachable while unpatched, the kernel-worker-spawned shell is the compromise check.
Defender takeaway
On NFS servers, restrict TCP 2049 to trusted networks, the step OpenSec, watchTowr and Red Hat all name, or stop nfs-server where it is not needed (Red Hat, 2026-11-26); turning off NFSv4.1 and 4.2 is the researchers' mitigation and no vendor endorses it. Then install the first distribution kernel that lists the CVE and reboot. A host that does not run nfsd is outside the exposure the sources describe.

item.title: SoftwareOK Q-Dir and DesktopOK installers carried a Python RAT; check hashes, reinstalling may not remove it
item.description: AhnLab ASEC reports that Q-Dir 12.83.0.0 to 12.85.0.0 and DesktopOK 12.82.0.0 and 12.85.0.0 installers distributed from SoftwareOK's official site were tampered with and install a Python remote-access tool that compares running processes with 1,206 security-product names. ASEC says copies updated through the update function may be affected, has not found how the files were replaced, and the vendor's pages carry no notice as of 2026-11-27.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

SoftwareOK: Q-Dir 12.83 to 12.85 and DesktopOK 12.82 and 12.85 installers from the vendor's official site carried a Python remote-access tool, ASEC says the update function may have been affected too, and reinstalling may not remove it

AhnLab's ASEC reports that Q-Dir 12.83.0.0, 12.84.0.0 and 12.85.0.0 and DesktopOK 12.82.0.0 and 12.85.0.0 were replaced with tampered installers on SoftwareOK's official distribution path, and that the SHA-256 of some files downloaded from the official site did not match the value posted on its download page. ASEC says the evidence indicates malicious files were also generated during the update process of installed copies, a point it later hedges (users of the update function "may have been affected"), and that it has not identified how the files were replaced (ASEC, 2026-11-25).

The tampered installer embeds the genuine, correctly signed Q-Dir or DesktopOK executable and runs it from the public user folder so the program appears to work. It then downloads the legitimate 7-Zip console extractor and a package holding a Python runtime and a remote-access tool, unpacks it under a Microsoft-looking folder in ProgramData and persists through a scheduled task, named to look like Edge, that runs the windowless Python interpreter. The tool runs shell commands and Python code, transfers files, takes screenshots and collects system information, and it compares running processes with a list of 1,206 security-product process names and sends the matches to its server. ASEC does not describe the server protocol, names no malware family or actor, and reads Chinese-language comments in the code only as a hint (ASEC, 2026-11-25).

ASEC gives no distribution window. SoftwareOK's release pages date Q-Dir 12.83 to 4 November, 12.84 to 13 November and 12.85 to 21 November (SoftwareOK, 2026-11-21) and DesktopOK 12.82 to 28 October and 12.85 to 19 November (SoftwareOK, 2026-11-26), which bounds only when the listed versions could first have reached users, and its Q-Dir download page carries no notice about tampering as of 2026-11-27 (SoftwareOK, 2026-11-27).

Exposure
Any Windows endpoint on which the listed versions were installed or updated since 2026-10-28; ASEC adds that other versions installed or updated while the tampered files were distributed may be affected. The installed program is the genuine signed one, so a signature check on it passes; the check that finds the tampering is the installer's SHA-256 against the vendor page.
Detection
Software-inventory telemetry for the listed versions; in scheduled-task creation and process-creation telemetry, a task running a bundled Python interpreter from under ProgramData and an extractor tool started by an installer; and egress from that interpreter. After removal ASEC says to look for the Python environment, scheduled tasks, related files and external connections.
Defender takeaway
Treat every host that ran an affected installer or updater as compromised: isolate it, remove the tool and rotate the credentials used on it, because ASEC says uninstalling and reinstalling the utility may not remove the remote-access tool.
incident27 Nov 04:41Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: AhnLab ASEC · SoftwareOK

item.title: Update: Java4Shell: OpenJDK Base64 heap overflow chained to pre-auth RCE in Jira and Keycloak; update Java, attempts seen
item.description: HPE Networking's bulletin HPESBNW05193 lists Central On-Premises, New Central On-Premises, NetEdit, Analytics and Location Engine, AirWave, ClearPass 6.14.x and SD-WAN Orchestrator 9.7.x as affected, with fixes for AirWave and Orchestrator, a ClearPass fix expected on 2026-12-01, a hypervisor-level workaround and a flag check; Cisco's advisory is at version 1.4.
item.content:encoded:
Update26 Nov 2026 05:07 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-intelsummarysourcesaffected_productsentitiescvesbodyupdated_at

HPE Networking's bulletin HPESBNW05193 lists Central On-Premises, New Central On-Premises, NetEdit, Analytics and Location Engine, AirWave, ClearPass 6.14.x and SD-WAN Orchestrator 9.7.x as affected, with fixes for AirWave and Orchestrator, a ClearPass fix expected on 2026-12-01, a hypervisor-level workaround and a flag check; Cisco's advisory is at version 1.4.

HPE Networking's bulletin HPESBNW05193 of 2026-11-25 (status Investigating) lists as known affected Central On-Premises 2.5.8 build 12 and below, New Central On-Premises 3.0.4.4 and below, NetEdit 2.19.0 and below, Analytics and Location Engine 5.2.0 and below, AirWave 8.3.0.7 and below, ClearPass Policy Manager 6.14.x and SD-WAN Orchestrator 9.7.x. It says exposure depends on the environment: an instance whose CPU does not expose the avx512vbmi feature is not vulnerable, which HPE checks with a search of /proc/cpuinfo for that flag (HPE Networking, 2026-11-25). Fixed builds are AirWave 8.3.0.8 and above, SD-WAN Orchestrator 9.7.2.41110 and 9.7.1.42066 and ClearPass 6.14.1-HF3 (expected 2026-12-01); Central On-Premises 2.5.8 build 13, NetEdit 2.19.1, Analytics and Location Engine 5.2.1 and the New Central On-Premises build have no date yet (HPE Networking, 2026-11-25).

HPE's workaround for virtual machines is to hide the avx512vbmi feature from the guest at the hypervisor (a per-VM mask or an EVC baseline of Skylake or Cascade Lake generation on VMware, and equivalent settings on QEMU/KVM, Proxmox, OpenStack Nova, Xen, VirtualBox and Firecracker), followed by a power cycle; Hyper-V cannot mask a single feature and public clouds need an instance family without VBMI. Central On-Premises, New Central On-Premises and bare-metal ClearPass cannot hide the flag, so HPE says to restrict management access to a dedicated segment or firewall policy, and it names no JVM option. HPE knows of no public discussion or exploit code against its products (HPE Networking, 2026-11-25).

Cisco's advisory now reads version 1.4: Catalyst Center, ISE, IOS XE, IOS XR and NX-OS read not affected, about 26 other products are listed as affected with the release or date still to be determined, patches for Secure Network Analytics are planned for 7.6.1, 7.6.0 and 7.5.3, and Cisco says no workaround addresses the vulnerability (Cisco, 2026-11-23). Siemens' advisory SSA-810379, at version 1.1 of 2026-11-23, adds Desigo CC Advanced Reporting V8 and V9 as affected with no fix (Siemens, 2026-11-19).

Open finding: Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938, OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later and Oracle Java SE on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI: a heap overflow in the Base64 decoder that Calif chains into pre-authentication code execution in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate; fixed in 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1, GreyNoise reports exploitation attempts, none confirmed successful against its sensors (CVSS 3.1 8.1) →

item.title: Update: nginx2root: five unauthenticated flaws reach worker RCE, Rapid7 PoC public; update to 1.31.10, 1.30.8, Plus 37.3.1.1
item.description: Unit 42 reached pre-authentication code execution through CVE-2026-123633 as the worker user in a two-VM lab, on a non-default configuration and chained with a memory leak F5 has not given a CVE, and publishes the exposure test and a log signal. Palo Alto Networks released its last three PAN-OS fixed builds and cleared 11.1 and 10.2, and Cisco's advisory, now at version 1.5, rates the flaws High and changes several product statuses and fixed releases.
item.content:encoded:
Update26 Nov 2026 05:07 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-intelsummaryactionssourcesbodyupdated_at

Unit 42 reached pre-authentication code execution through CVE-2026-123633 as the worker user in a two-VM lab, on a non-default configuration and chained with a memory leak F5 has not given a CVE, and publishes the exposure test and a log signal. Palo Alto Networks released its last three PAN-OS fixed builds and cleared 11.1 and 10.2, and Cisco's advisory, now at version 1.5, rates the flaws High and changes several product statuses and fixed releases.

Unit 42 published a first-person account of reaching pre-authentication code execution through CVE-2026-123633 as the non-root NGINX worker on a two-VM lab target running 1.31.8: the first attempt recovered a libc address without a shell and the second opened an interactive shell. The chain needed a non-default configuration and a separate memory disclosure that F5 assessed as limited to a non-typical configuration and has not given a CVE, whose details Unit 42 withholds (Unit 42, 2026-11-24). The tested path needs HTTP/2 on the listener and a reverse-proxy route whose upstream is a variable resolved at request time, with free worker connections at or below one sixteenth of worker_connections; static upstream routes still need review, and Unit 42 publishes no confirmed indicators of compromise. A log signal Unit 42 gives is the error-log warning that worker connections are not enough and are being reused, which needs the warn log level (Unit 42, 2026-11-24). Raising worker_connections adds only headroom and disabling HTTP/2 on some listeners leaves extra HTTP/1.1 connections, so neither replaces the upgrade; no source reports exploitation.

Palo Alto Networks removed the ETA for 12.1.7-h15, 11.2.10-h19 and 11.2.13-h6 on 2026-11-24 because those builds are released, so every fixed build named above is available, marked PAN-OS 11.1 and 10.2 as not impacted, and says the impacted products for CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-123634 and CVE-2026-113425 are the same as for the two HTTP/2 flaws; it knows of no malicious exploitation (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-20). Cisco's advisory, at version 1.5 of 2026-11-26 then, had rated the flaws High rather than Critical since version 1.2 of 2026-11-23, lists IOS XE as not affected, gives NX-OS 10.3.11, 10.4.9, 10.5.7, 10.6.5 and 10.7.1 in place of 10.7.2F, lists Catalyst Center with bug IDs and fixes 3.3.3 and 3.4.1 (dates to be determined) where it was listed as not affected, and writes the Finesse fix as 15.0(1)SU3 with Unified Intelligence Center on the same release (Cisco, 2026-11-20). Fortinet's advisory then listed FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer as not impacted and still had FortiAuthenticator and dozens of other products under investigation (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-20). Synology's SA-26:20, revised on 2026-11-24 and 2026-11-26, now lists fixed builds beyond DSM 7.4 and 7.3: 7.2.2-72806-11 for DSM 7.2.2, 7.2.1-69057-14 for DSM 7.2.1, 7.1.1-42962-10 for DSM 7.1 and 1.5.6-68000 for BeeStation OS 1.5, with only DSM Enterprise 1.0 still listed as ongoing (Synology, 2026-11-19).

Open finding: NGINX nginx2root: five unauthenticated memory-corruption flaws (CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 in HTTP/2, CVE-2026-121810 in HTTP/3, CVE-2026-123634 in the resolver, CVE-2026-113425 in the mail proxy) can lead to code execution as the worker process; fixed in nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 and NGINX Plus 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1, Rapid7 proof of concept public, no exploitation reported (CVSS 4.0 9.2) →

item.title: Update: PolinRider: forged backdated commits, npm hijacks and a fake recruiter run a loader at build or folder open
item.description: SafeDep found a Python variant of the loader in 375 public repositories, hidden in a utils package or conftest.py, and StepSecurity traced force-pushed pull-request commits that ran in CircuitVerse's release workflows and published 40 infected installers, with the loader padded by tabs; StepSecurity counts 576 infected repositories of 622 fetched.
item.content:encoded:
Update26 Nov 2026 05:07 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-intelsummarytechniquessourcessourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

SafeDep found a Python variant of the loader in 375 public repositories, hidden in a utils package or conftest.py, and StepSecurity traced force-pushed pull-request commits that ran in CircuitVerse's release workflows and published 40 infected installers, with the loader padded by tabs; StepSecurity counts 576 infected repositories of 622 fetched.

SafeDep reports that PolinRider now plants a Python loader in GitHub repositories, hidden in a small utils package or in conftest.py with five import lines added to a start file, and found it in 375 public repositories under 260 accounts on 2026-11-24; no PyPI or npm package carries it, and because it uses only the standard library a scan of requirements files or a lockfile does not show it (SafeDep, 2026-11-24). When Python imports the file, the loader reads the input data of the newest transaction an Ethereum wallet sent to itself, writes it as JavaScript to a temporary file and runs node on it; the next stage is written to the standard input of a detached interactive node process, so it is absent from the process command line, and the node child starts from python or pytest. pytest runs the loader through conftest.py every time, and fixing an import error for the missing utils package also starts it. SafeDep did not contact the command server, so later stages are unobserved, and the stealer behavior it describes comes from the September chain. Its remedy is to delete the planted package, import lines and conftest.py loader, then clean the machines that push to the repository and replace their GitHub tokens and SSH keys (SafeDep, 2026-11-24).

StepSecurity reports that the loader reached open-source projects through commits force-pushed on 2026-10-19 into pull requests that were still open, from one GitHub account, at AsyncAPI Generator, CircuitVerse and Open Food Facts; the malicious commits reuse a clean commit's message and date but are unsigned and carry a different committer name, and none of the merged pull requests contains the loader (StepSecurity, 2026-11-26). In the files it read, the added line is about 315 tab characters followed by the loader, so GitHub's diff looks empty, and the loader runs from a prefix on the build and dev scripts, from a Jest or PostCSS config file or from a hidden VS Code folder-open task. CircuitVerse's pull_request workflows ran on the poisoned fork commits with no approval step, and its maintainers confirmed the loader ran in the desktop build and deleted 40 installers that had stayed downloadable for more than a month; AsyncAPI's CI did not run it, and Open Food Facts' builds failed and its maintainers rotated a secret. StepSecurity counts 576 infected repositories of 622 it fetched, across 311 accounts, and assesses from a shared funding wallet that the fake interviews and these infections share an operator (StepSecurity, 2026-11-26).

Open finding: PolinRider: a North Korea-linked loader reaches developers through force-pushed forged commits in at least 7,609 GitHub repositories, hijacked npm releases and a fake employer's take-home test, and reads its server address from an Ethereum wallet →

item.content:encoded:
Update26 Nov 2026 05:06 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagssectorscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteclassificationactionsbodyupdated_at

watchTowr reports exploitation attempts against the GeoServer chain, in the form of error-based probes that create and invoke stored queries, and NCSC Switzerland rates the chain actively exploited; watchTowr is the only observer and the sources name different CVEs as exploited. The record also adds CVE-2026-120704, the SQLite JDBC extension-loading step that Eye Security's variant of the chain uses.

watchTowr reports that attackers are exploiting the chain: its vulnerability FAQ of 2026-11-25 says the flaws are being exploited in the wild, and The Hacker News quotes watchTowr that attackers sent error-based exploit probes that create and invoke stored queries to check whether a server is vulnerable (watchTowr, 2026-11-25; The Hacker News, 2026-11-25). The sources disagree on which flaws: The Hacker News names CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 in its lead and CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129244 in its quote of watchTowr, watchTowr's prose names all five chain CVEs, and its own table then marked only CVE-2026-129245 as exploited. NCSC Switzerland's advisory 13242 of 2026-11-25 rates the chain Actively Exploited with a proof of concept available, labels only CVE-2026-120705 as actively exploited and lists watchTowr's post as its source (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-25). No victim, actor or scale is named; the project's own pages make no exploitation statement.

Eye Security's disclosure uses a different last step, CVE-2026-120704, administrator-controlled loading of an SQLite JDBC extension that gives native code execution and is fixed in the same three releases (Eye Security, 2026-11-24); on Windows the project says the extension library can load from an SMB share, so nothing needs staging on the server (GeoServer, 2026-11-23). CVE-2026-120705 echoes file contents only when a layer is published to anonymous users, and its fix reaches embedders through GeoTools 35.2, 34.6 and 33.7 (GeoServer, 2026-11-23). On a cluster, set the same GEOSERVER_REMEMBERME_KEY on every node, because the fixed releases generate a new random remember-me key at each start (watchTowr, 2026-11-25).
