item.title: Update: FBI: various actors run ARTEX against many sectors, government included; Microsoft now names six users
item.description: Microsoft's defender guide of 2026-11-25 names six ARTEX users, adding the North Korean clusters Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet and the clusters Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, says ThreatBook sells an ARTEX Pro, and lists web-server, identity and egress detections; ThreatBook's own release presents the commercial edition as its product, which GTIG's fork description does not state.
item.content:encoded:
Update26 Nov 2026 05:05 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-intelheadlinesummarytagsentitiestechniquessourcesevidencebodyupdated_at

Microsoft's defender guide of 2026-11-25 names six ARTEX users, adding the North Korean clusters Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet and the clusters Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, says ThreatBook sells an ARTEX Pro, and lists web-server, identity and egress detections; ThreatBook's own release presents the commercial edition as its product, which GTIG's fork description does not state.

Microsoft's defender guide of 2026-11-25 says it has observed state-sponsored and financially motivated actors such as Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon integrating ARTEX into their tooling (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). For Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet the basis is Microsoft's report of 2026-10-29, which says it has identified both using ARTEX since late October 2026 and says that human operators likely continue to direct intent and objectives (Microsoft, 2026-10-29); the guide gives no campaign detail for Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, which The Record describes as Chinese state-backed groups (The Record, 2026-11-25). The Record also reports that The New York Times and Nextgov said ARTEX was allegedly used in attacks on the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (The Record, 2026-11-25). Nextgov, citing people familiar with the matter, says ARTEX is believed to have been used in the breach of an unclassified CIA and ODNI system for analyzing public and commercially available information and in an intrusion into the Defense Department's Cyber Defense Command, which one of its sources called low-impact, and that it is unclear who carried out the CIA and ODNI breach or whether information was taken (Nextgov, 2026-11-24).

Microsoft says ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November and began offering commercial access to an ARTEX Pro (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). ThreatBook's own launch release of 2026-10-16 already lists Artex Pro as an extension of the open-source Artex, developed as a personal project by the product lead of its RedAgents platform, and says the open-source edition was converted to closed source on 8 October 2026 after attackers misused it (Macau Business, 2026-10-16); GTIG lists ARTEX PRO among community forks, whereas ThreatBook's release presents it as the vendor's own extension, so the sources differ on whether it is a fork.

Microsoft says ARTEX can drive virtually any model, including open-weight and guardrail-stripped ones, and can switch models when one fails, so its activity is not necessarily constrained by any single provider's safety controls or visible in any single provider's telemetry; it adds that ARTEX introduces no new techniques and does not obfuscate by default, and calls behavior the most durable signal: a wide variety of requests in a brief time, retries of technique variants and next-stage actions at machine speed (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). Its detections, by telemetry class: on web servers, web-server processes (w3wp.exe, php-fpm, httpd or apache2, Java application servers) starting shells, script files created in web-accessible or upload directories, including files a database server process writes after its log file was pointed at a web directory, several short-lived web shells with incrementing names, and rapid reads of /etc/shadow, .env files, private keys and cloud credential files; in access logs, a client requesting 100 or more distinct paths with 50 or more client errors in one minute; in Entra sign-in logs, one address attempting service-principal sign-ins for three or more applications within an hour with both failures and successes, where a success after an invalid or expired client secret error warrants immediate investigation; in the audit log, one identity adding application credentials and assigning roles or permissions within an hour, and in one case an application assigning itself Global Administrator; and on egress, reverse shells and requests from servers to webhook and file-sharing services, where Microsoft's lever is to restrict outbound connections from web servers (Microsoft, 2026-11-25).

Microsoft's thresholds are defaults to tune: exclude build and automation servers that run shells under Java or Node.js, review file names because content management system updates also write script files, and do not alert on default curl, Wget, Python or headless Chromium user agents alone (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). Service-principal sign-ins are logged separately from interactive ones, so an empty hunt proves nothing where they are not collected (Microsoft, 2026-11-25).

Open finding: ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration →

item.title: 1Password breach via an employee GitHub account exported customer records; vaults not affected
item.description: 1Password disclosed on 2026-11-25 that an attacker who had gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account pushed malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data about a subset of customers: names, email addresses, identifiers, public keys, protocol parameters and tokens embedded in some emailed invitation, provisioning and account-recovery links. The attacker also copied private-repository source code and reached the CI/CD system, and 1Password rotated every credential that may have been exposed. 1Password says vault contents, vault keys and recovery keys were not affected and the exposed tokens need an SSO sign-in or an emailed code, which it lengthened; it does not say how the account was compromised or how many customers are affected.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

1Password: an attacker used an employee's corporate GitHub account to push malicious code to backend services that downloaded administrative data about a subset of customers, and copied private-repository source code and reached the CI/CD system; vaults were not affected

1Password disclosed on 2026-11-25 that on 2026-11-19 it began investigating indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account (1Password, 2026-11-25). The attacker used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data about customers; the attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the CI/CD system, which holds infrastructure secrets, and 1Password rotated every credential that may have been exposed (1Password, 2026-11-25). It says the actor had stolen a token and that vault contents, the keys that protect them, account recovery keys and its apps and browser extensions were not affected (1Password, 2026-11-25).

The records taken for a subset of users, whose size is not stated, are names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, tokens embedded in certain emailed invitation, SCIM Bridge and Hosted Provisioning, and account-recovery links, and non-secret internal metadata (1Password, 2026-11-25). Those tokens complete an invitation or recovery only together with an SSO sign-in or an emailed code, which 1Password has lengthened from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters, and it says it found no evidence of account takeover with the exposed tokens; its advice to customers is caution about phishing that mentions invitations or account recovery, that it will never ask for the account password or Secret Key, keeping both safe, and reporting suspicious messages to its support address (1Password, 2026-11-25). BleepingComputer adds that the harvested name and email list is useful for such phishing (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
Any organisation with 1Password accounts, since users' names, sign-in addresses and identifiers were in the copied records, and especially one using SCIM provisioning or account recovery, because tokens in those emailed links were among the data; 1Password says it notified a small number of users with pending invitations or recoveries directly (1Password, 2026-11-25).
Detection
In the identity provider's and 1Password's administrator audit records, invitation, provisioning and account-recovery events since about 2026-11-19 that no administrator or user requested; in mail-gateway logs, inbound mail that imitates 1Password invitations or recovery messages with real tenant or user details; and user reports of recovery codes nobody asked for. These checks are analysis from the data classes the post lists, which publishes no indicator.

Triage: a legitimate invitation or recovery message follows an administrator's or user's own action; one that arrives without it is the signal.

Defender takeaway
1Password's own advice covers phishing caution, never sharing the password or Secret Key and reporting suspicious messages, and BleepingComputer says it is not requiring customers to change their account passwords or Secret Keys (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-25); the action is to warn users about phishing that mentions invitations or account recovery and to watch for unrequested provisioning events. For your own pipelines the mechanism is one employee source-control identity that could push to backend services and reach CI/CD, so require review on the deploy path and alert on pushes and workflow changes made with employee tokens.

item.title: Juniper Session Smart Conductor: unauthenticated root command injection exploited; upgrade to 7.0.5, 7.1.7 or 7.2.3
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-103406 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-25, after BSI revised its advisory to say the flaw is being exploited. ENISA's record, which carries Juniper's own description, calls it an OS command injection in the AutomatedProvisioner of Session Smart Conductor that lets a remote attacker run commands as root through a crafted salt minion ID (CVSS 3.1 9.8, no privileges or user interaction), with the affected ranges ending at 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3. Juniper's bulletin JSA112183 was updated on 2026-11-24 to say at least one malicious exploitation was reported to its security response team, as SecurityWeek quotes it (the bulletin page itself could not be read); no source names an actor, victim or scale.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-103406 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-103406, Juniper Session Smart Conductor before 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3: an unauthenticated OS command injection as root through a crafted salt minion ID in the AutomatedProvisioner (CVSS 3.1 9.8) is exploited: Juniper says at least one malicious exploitation was reported to it, BSI reported exploitation and CISA listed it on 2026-11-25

CISA added CVE-2026-103406 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-25 (CISA, 2026-11-25); the catalogue record says a remote attacker could execute arbitrary commands as root via a specially crafted salt minion ID and names both Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router (CISA KEV catalogue, 2026-11-25). BSI had revised its advisory on 2026-11-24 (23:00 UTC) with the summary "CVE-2026-103406 is being exploited" (translated from German), without stating its basis (BSI, 2026-11-24). Juniper itself updated its bulletin JSA112183 on 2026-11-24 to say that at least one instance of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 has been reported to its security response team, as SecurityWeek quotes it (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-26), and NCSC Switzerland rates the flaw actively exploited (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26). No source names an actor, a victim or the number of compromised systems, and the only first-exploitation date, ENISA's exploited-since field of 2026-11-25, follows the catalogue listing (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-28).

ENISA's record, which carries Juniper's description, narrows the flaw to the AutomatedProvisioner of Session Smart Conductor: an improper neutralization of special elements lets a remote attacker execute arbitrary commands as root via a specially crafted salt minion ID, scored CVSS 3.1 9.8 with network access, no privileges and no user interaction (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-28). The affected ranges are Conductor before 7.0.5, from 7.1.0 before 7.1.7 and from 7.2.0 before 7.2.3, so 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3 are the first fixed releases (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-28). The record references Juniper's bulletin JSA112183, which could not be read, and its CVE record was published on 2026-10-28. The same release fixes CVE-2026-103409 in the Session Smart Router, an unauthenticated flaw scored 9.8 that can be exploited only before the device is onboarded to Mist or a Conductor (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A Session Smart Conductor on a release below 7.0.5, 7.1.7 or 7.2.3 that a network attacker can reach; NCSC Switzerland names network access to the Conductor's provisioning service (the AutomatedProvisioner) as the prerequisite, with no authentication or user interaction, and no source gives the port or says whether it is on by default (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26). CISA's catalogue record and NCSC.ch also name Session Smart Router, and SecurityWeek lists 7.2.3, 7.1.7 and 7.0.5 for both products (CISA KEV catalogue, 2026-11-25; SecurityWeek, 2026-11-26), so read the running release on each Conductor and each Router and compare it with the three fixed releases.
Detection
Process-creation events showing a shell or interpreter started as root by the Conductor's provisioning or salt services, minion or router registration events whose ID contains shell metacharacters or command-substitution syntax, and the Conductor's audit and configuration-change records; these follow from the mechanism ENISA relays, and no source publishes an indicator. Upgrading does not remove an attacker who is already in, so a Conductor that was reachable before the upgrade needs a check for accounts, router registrations and configuration pushed from it that nobody made; NCSC Switzerland's check is the fleet list, for router names the team did not create (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade every Conductor to a fixed release now rather than at the next cycle, since Juniper, CISA and BSI report exploitation of an unauthenticated root command injection; until then, NCSC Switzerland advises keeping the Conductor's management and provisioning interfaces off untrusted network segments (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26), because the flaw needs only network access.
Update27 Nov 2026 04:51 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-inteltitlesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

Juniper updated its bulletin JSA112183 on 2026-11-24, before CISA's listing, to say "At least one instance of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 has been reported to the Juniper SIRT" and to urge customers to upgrade to a fixed release as soon as possible and in the meantime mitigate; the bulletin page itself could not be read, so the wording is SecurityWeek's quotation (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-26). NCSC Switzerland's post of 2026-11-26 rates the flaw actively exploited and says the router ID a joining device supplies is passed unsanitised into a shell command during provisioning key setup, so that root on the Conductor exposes every managed router and its provisioning keys; it relays that Juniper lists no official workaround and advises keeping the Conductor's management and provisioning interfaces off untrusted network segments and auditing the fleet list for router names the team did not create (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26). Neither source names an actor, a victim or a count of compromised systems.

item.title: SEPPmail 15.1.2 fixes unauthenticated GINA account takeover (9.3) and ten more flaws; update the gateway
item.description: SEPPmail's patch release 15.1.2 of 2026-11-24 fixes eleven flaws in Secure E-Mail Gateway versions before 15.1.2, led by CVE-2026-130637 (vendor score 9.3): request values reflected on the GINA login page were processed by the template engine, which could let an unauthenticated attacker read attributes of any GINA account and take it over. Two more rows score 9.2 (a security-question recovery session accepted by the password-change workflows, and a hard-coded fallback secret for Large File Transfer attachments) and an unauthenticated request could reset a registered account's password without the security question. SEPPmail names no exploitation and no workaround, and does not say whether the 15.0 branch is affected.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-130637 +10NATOA2

SEPPmail Secure E-Mail Gateway before 15.1.2: an unauthenticated template injection on the GINA login page can read and take over any GINA account (CVE-2026-130637, vendor score 9.3) and ten more flaws are fixed in the 2026-11-24 patch release; no exploitation or workaround stated

SEPPmail's revision history lists patch release 15.1.2 of 2026-11-24 with eleven security fixes, each marked as affecting versions before 15.1.2 (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24). The worst is CVE-2026-130637 (vendor score 9.3): request values reflected on the GINA login page were processed by the template engine, which could let an unauthenticated attacker read attributes of any GINA account and take it over, and the fix stops expanding request values as template placeholders. Two further rows score 9.2: CVE-2026-124840, where a session created by answering the security question was also accepted by the registration and settings workflows, so an attacker who knows the security answer could replace the password, and CVE-2026-124843, where a hard-coded fallback secret was used if the appliance's key material could not be loaded, which could let encrypted Large File Transfer attachments be decrypted outside the appliance (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24).

The remaining rows are CVE-2026-124844 (8.7), unauthenticated GINA uploads that were never removed and could fill the disk; CVE-2026-124838 (8.5), a configuration-service socket open to every local user; CVE-2026-124842 (8.3), an unauthenticated GINA request that reset the password of a registered account without the security question; CVE-2026-124839 (7.7), a crafted GINA account address that reached a shell command in a maintenance script at start, with elevated privileges; and four rows at 6.9 to 6.3 covering unescaped LDAP filter values (CVE-2026-124841, CVE-2026-124836), a crafted DKIM signature that injects forged Authentication-Results later covered by the gateway's ARC seal (CVE-2026-124837) and a GINA domain lookup that falls back to the default domain settings (CVE-2026-124845) (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24). The page names no exploitation and no workaround, and does not say whether the 15.0 branch, whose last release is 15.0.7, is affected.

Exposure
A SEPPmail Secure E-Mail Gateway before 15.1.2 whose GINA web interface is reachable from outside; the revision history says release 15.1.0 added support for restricting the file types that external communication partners can upload through GINA, which shows external recipients use it (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24). The page does not state the CVSS vector of any score.
Detection
In GINA web access logs, login-page requests whose parameters carry template placeholder syntax, unauthenticated password-reset requests for accounts that are already registered, calls to the registration and settings workflows that follow a security-question recovery, and bursts of unauthenticated uploads; in the gateway's audit log, GINA password changes without the usual recovery sequence. The fixes do not undo an account already taken over, so review GINA password-change and sign-in history for the period before the update. These checks follow from the mechanisms the vendor names; the page publishes no indicator.

Triage: an unauthenticated password reset on a GINA account that is not yet registered is legitimate, since the fix keeps it for unregistered accounts only; the same request taking effect on an already registered account without the security-question step is the abuse (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24).

Defender takeaway
Update every gateway on 15.1 to 15.1.2 and, for gateways on the 15.0 branch, ask SEPPmail whether these flaws apply, since the page does not say; where GINA is internet-facing, give the update priority within the regular cycle, because the template injection and the unauthenticated reset need no login, and review GINA account changes made before the update.

item.title: Okta: AI agents sign up with mail.tm; its rotating domain will very likely outdate blocklists within weeks
item.description: Okta Threat Intelligence, with data from the P0 Labs team of Permiso (now part of Okta), reports that since June 2026, and at scale in October and November, AI agents registered accounts with disposable addresses, mostly from the mail.tm family, on Auth0 tenants and Okta organizations that allow public self-service registration. mail.tm exposes one active domain at a time through an account-free API and replaces it periodically, so a blocklist will very likely stop matching within weeks. Okta reads such sign-ups as a likely early sign that agents are tasked against an organization, and says agents often register through the Auth0 Authentication API, which can skip protections applied in Universal Login.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Okta Threat Intelligence: AI agents register on Auth0 tenants and Okta organizations with disposable addresses from the mail.tm service, whose single rotating mailbox domain makes blocklists very likely stop matching within weeks; ARTEX, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and pentestcode each picked it at run time

Okta Threat Intelligence reports that since June 2026, and at scale through October and November, AI agents have registered accounts with disposable email addresses on Auth0 tenants and Okta organizations that allow public self-service registration, activity Okta calls almost certainly malicious and that customers often reported alongside attacks on their applications (Okta, 2026-11-23). The addresses mostly belong to the mail.tm family, a free receive-only service whose API needs no account or key and lets a script create a mailbox, obtain a token and poll for one-time codes (Okta, 2026-11-23). In tests by the P0 Labs team of Permiso, which Okta acquired on 2026-08-26 (Okta, 2026-07-30), the ARTEX, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and pentestcode frameworks each picked mail.tm at run time, and in a data set containing attacker tooling mail.tm appeared on 80 percent of the attacker hosts where disposable email was found (Okta, 2026-11-23).

mail.tm exposes only one active mailbox domain at a time and replaces it periodically, so a blocklist built from earlier domains will very likely stop matching within weeks; Okta's Auth0 telemetry shows sign-ups tracking the domain the API currently returns, and the attackers' domain changed around 2026-10-30 when the API response did. Agents also used mailinator, guerrillamail and emailnator, and at one target an agent moved to another provider when blocked, which Okta reads as agents treating disposable mail as an interchangeable capability. Okta says the use always occurred within a short window of other agentic reconnaissance and intrusion attempts against the same entities (Okta, 2026-11-23). Bot detection and CAPTCHA generally stopped the October mail.tm sign-ups before email verification, but Okta warns agents can solve challenges and commonly register by calling the Auth0 Authentication API directly, which can skip protections applied in Universal Login (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
An Auth0 tenant or Okta organization that allows public self-service registration. For workforce users Okta says self-service registration is a prerequisite for many of the attacks it describes and should be disabled or restricted (Okta, 2026-11-23).
Detection
In identity-provider registration telemetry, sign-up events whose email domain belongs to a disposable provider's currently active mailbox domain, kept current by polling the provider's public domain endpoint instead of a static list, as Okta advises (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Triage: the discriminator Okta supports is context: a disposable-domain sign-up read alongside other agentic reconnaissance or intrusion attempts against the same entities, not the domain alone (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Defender takeaway
On Auth0, block sign-ups through the API while allowing Universal Login and block disposable domains with Actions; on Okta Workforce Identity, disable or restrict self-service registration. Treat a disposable-domain sign-up as a prompt to look for other agentic activity against the same estate, since Okta says it gives a heads-up to look for successful intrusion attempts, and do not rely on CAPTCHA alone (Okta, 2026-11-23).

item.title: Splunk Enterprise: unauthenticated REST bypasses accept an empty pass4SymmKey (CVSS 9.4, 9.1); set the key, upgrade
item.description: Splunk's SVD-2026-1103 of 2026-11-18 fixes 38 flaws in Splunk Enterprise, among them unauthenticated authentication bypasses in the REST API that rest on an empty shared secret: CVE-2026-76536 (CVSS 3.1 9.4, reads and changes clustering configuration on a standalone instance) and CVE-2026-76535 (9.1, runs search queries as an authenticated user), plus three rows at 7.5, two on an empty or factory-default shared key and one that crashes splunkd. Splunk lists fixes in 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12 and 9.4.17 and a workaround of setting a non-empty pass4SymmKey; it does not say an empty secret is the out-of-the-box state, and no source reports exploitation.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-76536 +3NATOA2

Splunk Enterprise SVD-2026-1103: two unauthenticated REST API authentication bypasses that accept an empty shared secret (CVE-2026-76536 in the cluster configuration endpoint, CVSS 3.1 9.4; CVE-2026-76535 in RapidDiag task collection, which runs searches as an authenticated user, 9.1) and three more unauthenticated rows at 7.5; fixed in 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12 and 9.4.17, no exploitation reported

Splunk's advisory SVD-2026-1103 of 2026-11-18 fixes 38 flaws in Splunk Enterprise, two rated Critical and unauthenticated (Splunk, 2026-11-18). CVE-2026-76536 (CVSS 3.1 9.4) lets an unauthenticated user use an empty clustering shared secret to read and modify clustering configuration through the cluster configuration REST endpoint on a standalone instance with clustering turned off, and CVE-2026-76535 (9.1) lets an unauthenticated user run arbitrary SPL searches through RapidDiag task collection as an authenticated user, because Splunk Enterprise accepts an empty shared secret on those requests (Splunk, 2026-11-18). Three further unauthenticated rows are rated 7.5: CVE-2026-131192 gives access to live event data from the indexing pipeline on a standalone instance or a search head that is not an indexer cluster member, on an empty shared key, and CVE-2026-131190 exposes RapidDiag process metadata and a log file inventory through endpoints that accept a factory-default shared key, and a third lets an unauthenticated user crash the Splunk daemon through the S2S data-forwarding receiver, for which Splunk lists no workaround (Splunk, 2026-11-18).

Splunk lists fixes in 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12 and 9.4.17, with CVE-2026-76536 and CVE-2026-131190 not listed for the 10.6 branch (Splunk, 2026-11-18). For CVE-2026-76535 Splunk says to set a non-empty pass4SymmKey in server.conf, using the same value on each node that participates in the service, and restart; for CVE-2026-76536 the workaround is a strong, unique pass4SymmKey of at least 12 characters in the [clustering] stanza of server.conf, standalone instances included, followed by a restart; CVE-2026-131190 is closed by turning off or removing the RapidDiag app (Splunk, 2026-11-18). The advisory does not say any flaw is exploited; NCSC-NL rates the likelihood medium and the damage high (NCSC-NL, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
A Splunk Enterprise instance whose pass4SymmKey is empty or unset (for CVE-2026-131190, one that accepts RapidDiag's factory-default key) and whose management REST API can be reached by an untrusted host; Splunk does not say an empty secret is the default on a stock install, so the effective value in server.conf is the thing to read on each instance, and Splunk Cloud impact is not addressed in the advisory.
Defender takeaway
Set a non-empty pass4SymmKey on every Splunk Enterprise instance now, since that is the workaround for the two Critical rows, and take the upgrade at the next window if the management API is internal; instances reachable from user or internet networks are the ones to do first.

item.title: GeoServer RCE chain: public PoC, CISA lists two flaws as exploited; update to 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7
item.description: The GeoServer project published a batch of security advisories on 2026-11-23, most for flaws fixed in 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7, and five of them chain an anonymous WFS request to code execution: a path disclosure, a service-security bypass with a prefixed service name, an XML injection, a predictable remember-me key that forges an administrator session (critical, CVSS 4.0 9.2) and a JDBC deserialization. The reporter, who says it works on a default installation, published a full-chain proof of concept the same day; the project announced the fixed releases on 2026-10-19. CISA added CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-27 on evidence of active exploitation it does not describe, watchTowr reports exploitation attempts in the form of error-based probes that create and invoke stored queries, and NCSC Switzerland rates the chain actively exploited.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-129244 +5exploitedupdatedNATOA2

GeoServer 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7: a five-step chain from an anonymous WFS request to code execution (CVE-2026-129244, CVE-2026-129243, CVE-2026-120705, CVE-2026-129245, CVE-2026-129242) works on a default installation, was disclosed in advisories published on 2026-11-23 and has a public proof of concept; CISA lists CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 as exploited, and watchTowr reports exploitation attempts, which NCSC Switzerland relays as actively exploited (CVSS 4.0 9.2 for the critical step)

The GeoServer project published a batch of security advisories on 2026-11-23, most for flaws fixed in 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7, which the project had announced on 2026-10-19 as an important upgrade for production systems (GeoServer, 2026-11-23; GeoServer, 2026-10-19). Five chain, in the order the project gives: a WFS stored-query exception that discloses the data directory path (CVE-2026-129244), service-security rules bypassed with a prefixed service name such as x/WFS so anonymous users can create stored queries (CVE-2026-129243), an unauthenticated WFS GetFeatureById XML injection (CVE-2026-120705), a predictable remember-me key that allows administrator session forgery (CVE-2026-129245, critical) and deserialization in the JDBC user and role services (CVE-2026-129242, administrator required) (GeoServer, 2026-11-23; GeoServer, 2026-11-23). The project says the critical advisory was first reported as step 4 of an unauthenticated remote command execution chain and that each step was given its own CVE at the CVE Numbering Authority's request (GeoServer, 2026-11-23).

The reporter says the chain gives unauthenticated remote command execution on a default installation: the service-name bypass lets an anonymous stored query read the files that hold the remember-me key and an administrator password digest, which forges an administrator session (CryptoCat, 2026-11-23). A full-chain proof of concept has been public since the reporter's write-up. Affected are 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5 and 2.27.6 and earlier, with 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7 as the fixed releases (GeoServer, 2026-11-23); the project says the 2.27 series has reached end of life (GeoServer, 2026-10-19). CISA lists CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 as exploited, and watchTowr reports exploitation attempts, which NCSC Switzerland rated actively exploited on 2026-11-25 (CISA, 2026-11-27; NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
GeoServer on the affected builds with WFS reachable by anonymous users and the REST API reachable; the reporter says it works on a default installation, with the stock admin account enabled in the default user service and, for its payload, a Linux host, and that the chain read the live key, so it never depended on the shipped value and a rotated key alone does not close it (CryptoCat, 2026-11-23); the fixed releases use a random per-node key and invalidate existing remember-me cookies on upgrade (GeoServer, 2026-11-23).
Detection
In web access logs, WFS requests whose service parameter contains a slash such as x/WFS, and stored queries you did not create under the data directory's wfs/query and workspaces/*/wfs/query folders (GeoServer, 2026-11-23); in REST access logs, an administrator session that uploads a database file and creates a JDBC user group service (GeoServer, 2026-11-23). If exposure is suspected the project advises changing administrator passwords, because changing the key does not help when the same file disclosure also reveals it (GeoServer, 2026-11-23).
Defender takeaway
Update internet-reachable GeoServer to a fixed release now rather than at the next cycle, since a public full-chain proof of concept exists, CISA lists two of the chain's flaws as exploited and the fixes are weeks old; where it must wait, apply the project's workarounds for steps 2 and 4, and on any instance that ran an older build while reachable, review the stored-query folders and the administrator accounts.
Update26 Nov 2026 05:06 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagssectorscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteclassificationactionsbodyupdated_at

watchTowr reports that attackers are exploiting the chain: its vulnerability FAQ of 2026-11-25 says the flaws are being exploited in the wild, and The Hacker News quotes watchTowr that attackers sent error-based exploit probes that create and invoke stored queries to check whether a server is vulnerable (watchTowr, 2026-11-25; The Hacker News, 2026-11-25). The sources disagree on which flaws: The Hacker News names CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 in its lead and CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129244 in its quote of watchTowr, watchTowr's prose names all five chain CVEs, and its own table then marked only CVE-2026-129245 as exploited. NCSC Switzerland's advisory 13242 of 2026-11-25 rates the chain Actively Exploited with a proof of concept available, labels only CVE-2026-120705 as actively exploited and lists watchTowr's post as its source (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-25). No victim, actor or scale is named; the project's own pages make no exploitation statement.

Eye Security's disclosure uses a different last step, CVE-2026-120704, administrator-controlled loading of an SQLite JDBC extension that gives native code execution and is fixed in the same three releases (Eye Security, 2026-11-24); on Windows the project says the extension library can load from an SMB share, so nothing needs staging on the server (GeoServer, 2026-11-23). CVE-2026-120705 echoes file contents only when a layer is published to anonymous users, and its fix reaches embedders through GeoTools 35.2, 34.6 and 33.7 (GeoServer, 2026-11-23). On a cluster, set the same GEOSERVER_REMEMBERME_KEY on every node, because the fixed releases generate a new random remember-me key at each start (watchTowr, 2026-11-25).

Update28 Nov 2026 04:50 UTCrun 2026-11-28T0355Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitle

CISA added CVE-2026-120705, the unauthenticated XML injection in the WFS GetFeatureById stored query, and CVE-2026-129243, the service-level authorization bypass through a prefixed service name, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-27, saying it did so on evidence of active exploitation (CISA, 2026-11-27). CISA names no actor, victim, scale or source for that evidence, so whether it saw watchTowr's activity or its own cannot be told. The alert lists only those two GeoServer flaws, so the status of the other three still rests on watchTowr: its FAQ table now marks CVE-2026-129245, CVE-2026-129243 and CVE-2026-120705 as exploited and CVE-2026-129244 and CVE-2026-129242 as not reported, while its prose says all five are being exploited in the wild (watchTowr, 2026-11-25).

item.title: Broadcom VMSA-2026-0011: second vCenter auth bypass and ESX I/O filter RCE, all 9.8; the earlier fix does not cover 9.x
item.description: Broadcom's VMSA-2026-0011 of 2026-11-24 fixes 23 flaws, among them CVE-2026-123903, a second authentication bypass in vCenter's Directory Service that needs only network access (CVSS 3.1 9.8, no workaround), and CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911, I/O filter service flaws in ESX that give code execution from network access (9.8 each). vCenter 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 and 8.0 U3m fix the vCenter flaw, so a 9.x vCenter already on the build that fixed the exploited CVE-2026-123890 (9.1.1.0200 or 9.0.2.0200) is still affected; no source reports exploitation of these 23 flaws.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-123903 +3NATOA2

VMSA-2026-0011, VMware vCenter and ESX: a second Directory Service authentication bypass in vCenter (CVE-2026-123903) and two I/O filter service flaws in ESX that give code execution from network access (CVE-2026-123910, CVE-2026-123911), all CVSS 3.1 9.8; no workaround for vCenter, fixed in vCenter 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 and 8.0 U3m, no exploitation reported

Broadcom's VMSA-2026-0011 of 2026-11-24 fixes 23 flaws across vCenter, ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools and Avi Load Balancer, rated Critical, and Broadcom's questions and answers treat the critical issues as an emergency change (Broadcom, 2026-11-24). CVE-2026-123903 is an authentication bypass in vCenter's VMware Directory Service, CVSS 3.1 9.8, reachable with network access to vCenter and no credentials, with no workaround; Broadcom calls it a new and distinct issue from the exploited CVE-2026-123890 in the same component (Broadcom, 2026-11-24; Broadcom, 2026-11-24). CVE-2026-123910 (heap out-of-bounds write) and CVE-2026-123911 (use-after-free) are flaws in the ESX I/O filter service, each 9.8 with network access to the host, and CVE-2026-123912 is an out-of-bounds write in the XHCI USB controller that gives code execution as the VMX process to an administrator inside a virtual machine, CVSS 9.3 in Workstation and Fusion and 8.4 in ESX (Broadcom, 2026-11-24).

Fixed builds: vCenter 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 and 8.0 U3m, VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x through 5.2.5 (KB88287), with no public fix for vCenter 7.0 or ESX 7.0; ESX ESXi-9.1.2.0-25946735, ESXi-9.0.2.0200-25953133 and ESXi80U3m-25926933; Workstation and Fusion 26H1u1 (Broadcom, 2026-11-24). Broadcom says a vCenter on 8.0 U3m from the earlier advisory needs no further update but vCenter 9.1.x does, and for 9.0.x the fixed version in the new advisory (9.0.2.0300) governs, so 9.1.1.0200 and 9.0.2.0200 do not carry the fix (Broadcom, 2026-11-24). For ESX 8.x only, KB463535 restricts TCP 9080, where the I/O filter service listens, to the vCenter address; Broadcom says limiting access to the service resolves only a small portion of the issues in the advisory and may affect cluster operation, and tells customers to apply the updates (Broadcom, 2026-11-24; Broadcom, 2026-11-24). Broadcom's release notes disagree with its response matrices in places: the vCenter 9.1.2 notes list only four vCenter CVEs, not the authentication bypass that the matrix says 9.1.2 fixes (Broadcom, 2026-11-24), the 8.0 U3m notes list only the earlier exploited flaw (Broadcom, 2026-11-19) and the 9.0.2.0300 notes list ESX flaws (Broadcom, 2026-11-24), and the questions and answers score CVE-2026-123912 at 8.5 for ESX where the response matrix prints 8.4, and Broadcom names the advisory as the source of truth for affected versions and patches (Broadcom, 2026-11-24). Neither the advisory nor the questions and answers say any flaw is exploited, and no source reports it as of 2026-11-25.

Exposure
Any vCenter Server reachable over the network, with the build shown in the appliance's version summary, and any ESX host whose I/O filter service port is reachable; on ESX 8.x that service listens on TCP 9080 and KB463535 says only vCenter should reach it.
Detection
Broadcom publishes no indicators. Flows to TCP 9080 on ESX hosts from any address other than the vCenter Server are outside the pattern KB463535 describes, and administrator sessions or account changes on a vCenter that was reachable before patching deserve the review described for the earlier Directory Service bypass.
Defender takeaway
Treat it as the emergency change Broadcom describes: move vCenter and ESX to the builds above, re-patch any 9.x vCenter that stopped at the earlier advisory's build, and keep management interfaces and the ESX I/O filter port off untrusted networks until then; vCenter 7.0 and ESX 7.0 have no public fix and Broadcom directs extended-support customers to its support, so isolation is the interim lever there.

item.title: Unit 42: AI agents behind web shells in 10+ campaigns; hunt 1.4 s command gaps and ===[Title]=== headers
item.description: Unit 42 tracked more than ten campaigns between July and September 2026 in which different attackers pointed autonomous AI agents at targets in sectors including government, logistics, manufacturing and education. Every campaign began with a web shell on a vulnerable web application, after which the agent did reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation and lateral movement mostly with single-use scripts and no compiled implants. Unit 42 reports no new technique but measurable traces: a median gap of 1.4 seconds between commands in a subset of attacks (23.9 seconds in the human phase), section headers such as ===[Title]=== in every campaign, and 40 to 100 unique Base64 payloads per session.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Unit 42: more than ten campaigns in July to September 2026 ran autonomous AI agents from web-shell footholds on vulnerable web applications, with a command-gap median of 1.4 seconds, ===[Title]=== script headers and 40 to 100 unique Base64 payloads per session

Unit 42 tracked more than ten global campaigns between July and September 2026 in which different attackers deployed autonomous AI agents, against sectors including government, logistics, manufacturing, agriculture and education. Every campaign began with a web shell deployed through a vulnerable web application, typically supplied by the human operator, after which the agent did reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation and lateral movement; Unit 42 names no product, CVE or flaw class for the entry vectors and says the novelty was speed and efficiency, not technique (Unit 42, 2026-11-24).

The traces: a median gap of 1.4 seconds between commands once an agent took over, against 23.9 seconds in the human phase of a subset of attacks; about 800 unique commands in 140 minutes in one case; section headers such as ===[Title]=== in shell commands and scripts in every campaign and step-by-step reasoning notes in more than half; 40 to 100 unique, target-tailored Base64 payloads per session; and no compiled implants, the arsenal being in most cases simple single-use scripts such as PHP web shells, PowerShell WMI backdoors and Python credential harvesters. The agents probed defences: the same find command ran on six endpoints excluding three security vendors, and one agent applied strace to the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint daemon (Unit 42, 2026-11-24).

The Copy Fail exploit recurred across several organisations; in a different attack sequence an agent tried the public PwnKit and CVE-2024-1086 binaries, then wrote custom C on the target and rewrote the exploit in Python, and Unit 42 saw agents try five techniques in sequence when earlier ones failed. In one AWS case it switched to IMDSv2 token acquisition after IMDSv1 was blocked and enumerated 20 services across eight regions; in another it pushed web shells to more than 40 locations on a Windows IIS server within 26 minutes, and Unit 42 describes another agent that found a vendor's GitLab credentials on a victim's web server and tried to brute-force access to that GitLab instance, exploiting no GitLab flaw (Unit 42, 2026-11-24).

Unit 42 found no behavioural marker tying the activity to a model or framework; a command-and-control address in one campaign also hosted a CyberStrikeAI instance, from which it infers the orchestration platform (Unit 42, 2026-11-24). ReliaQuest saw a credential-gated CyberStrikeAI login page on a staging host and could not determine whether the tool played a part (ReliaQuest, 2026-10-07).

Exposure
Internet-facing web servers that host a vulnerable web application; Unit 42 does not name the applications.
Detection
In process-lineage telemetry, shells and scripts spawned through a web shell's sh -c interface in bursts seconds apart, with ===[Title]=== headers or reasoning-style comments and many unique Base64 payloads; the same enumeration command across hosts excluding security-product directories, and tracing of the endpoint-security daemon; on cloud workloads, a switch to IMDSv2 token requests after IMDSv1 is blocked.

Triage: Base64 commands and reconnaissance appear in human-operated intrusions; Unit 42's discriminators are the volume and uniqueness of payloads, the command cadence and the headers, which it says rarely appear in human-operated attacks except with pre-coded scripts.

Defender takeaway
Hunt web-server hosts for these traces, looking for volumes of single-use scripts rather than malware families, and close the web-tier entry first; enforce MFA, sign-in rate limiting and source-address restriction on services whose credentials sit on web servers, as Unit 42 advises for GitLab.

item.title: BACS: five confirmed AI-agent attacks in Switzerland, three on critical infrastructure; critical updates within 24 hours
item.description: Switzerland's Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS) said on 2026-11-24 that it had for the first time received reports of attacks on Swiss companies and critical-infrastructure operators in at least two sectors that were carried out with the support of an AI agent; on 2026-11-26 its director told SRF that BACS has five confirmed cases, three on critical-infrastructure operators, and SRF reports that systems were compromised in four of the five (RTS reads two successes among three critical-infrastructure attacks, and BACS's page says every case known on 2026-11-24). No framework, sector, victim or entry point is named for the Swiss cases and the actor is unknown; BACS says the number of internet-reachable agents such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI has almost doubled since October 2026 and recommends critical updates on internet-reachable systems within 24 hours.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHupdatedNATOA2

BACS: first confirmed cyberattacks carried out with AI agents against Swiss companies and critical-infrastructure operators, five confirmed cases according to its director, three on critical-infrastructure operators; internet-reachable agents such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI have almost doubled since October

BACS reported on 2026-11-24 that in recent days it had received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland carried out with the support of an AI agent, that the victims are various companies and operators of critical infrastructure in at least two sectors, and that in every case known to it then the use of AI agents led to a successful compromise of the victim's IT systems (BACS, 2026-11-24). Its director told SRF on 2026-11-26 that BACS has five confirmed cases, three on critical-infrastructure operators, with SMEs that reported voluntarily also hacked, and SRF reports that systems were compromised in four of the five (translated from German) (SRF, 2026-11-26); RTS reads three critical-infrastructure attacks of which two succeeded, without saying whether the count covers all five (translated from French) (RTS, 2026-11-26). BACS calls these the first confirmed Swiss cases and says the attackers used so-called "Agentic Offensive Frameworks", agents that independently search for weaknesses, choose attack tools, evaluate the results and plan the next steps (BACS, 2026-11-24). Neither the page nor the two outlets name a framework used in these cases, a victim sector or an entry point; SRF reports no larger outages and an unknown actor, and BACS shares technical indicators for detecting such AI tools with critical-infrastructure operators (SRF, 2026-11-26; BACS, 2026-11-24). Netzwoche reported on 2026-11-02 that BACS's GovCERT co-head had said at the Gohack26 symposium that no case in which autonomous AI agents hacked someone had been reported to the office so far (translated from German) (Netzwoche, 2026-11-02).

Describing the tool class in general, BACS says such agents exploit, for example, standard or easily guessed passwords and known vulnerabilities in software or internet-connected systems, often need only a fraction of the time a human would to find and exploit vulnerable systems, and switch to other known attack methods when they meet a defence (BACS, 2026-11-24). It adds that the number of internet-reachable AI agents such as ARTEX or CyberStrikeAI has almost doubled since October 2026, with no baseline or counting method given, names the two tools only as examples and does not say they were used in the Swiss cases, and expects an accumulation of fast, successful attacks (BACS, 2026-11-24).

Exposure
Internet-reachable systems with standard or easily guessed passwords or with known, unpatched vulnerabilities, which is what BACS says such agents exploit; BACS addresses its recommendations to companies in Switzerland and does not name administrations or sectors.
Detection
BACS recommends detecting when identities, applications, workloads and infrastructure deviate from their established behaviour patterns (BACS, 2026-11-24); BACS says it shares technical indicators with critical-infrastructure operators and publishes none in the text.
Defender takeaway
BACS asks that critical security updates for internet-reachable systems be installed as soon as possible and at the latest after 24 hours (the BACS German text gives no start point; the official English page and SRF's report say after release) (BACS, 2026-11-24; SRF, 2026-11-26), that access to exposed systems be limited by allow-list or geo-blocking, and that MFA or passkeys cover every internet-reachable internal resource without exception (BACS, 2026-11-24). Check the internet-facing estate for default and guessable passwords and for patch lag against that 24-hour ceiling first.
Update28 Nov 2026 04:41 UTCrun 2026-11-28T0355Z-intelbodyevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytitle

BACS director Florian Schütz told SRF on 2026-11-26 that BACS currently has five confirmed cases of attacks with AI agents, all reported in recent days (translated from German) (SRF, 2026-11-26). SRF reports that three victims are operators of critical infrastructure and that SMEs that reported voluntarily were also hacked with the help of AI agents, that systems were successfully hacked in four of the five cases (indirect speech, with no named speaker for that sentence), that there had been no larger outages, that it is still unclear who is behind the attacks and that BACS will not name the victims, who have the right to communicate themselves, in Schütz's words (SRF, 2026-11-26). RTS, relaying the interview, reads three attacks on critical infrastructure of which two succeeded, without saying whether that count covers all five cases (translated from French) (RTS, 2026-11-26), while BACS's own page of 2026-11-24, unchanged on 2026-11-28, still says that every case known to it ended in a compromise (BACS, 2026-11-24). The three readings differ, so no single success ratio is a BACS finding. Neither SRF nor RTS says which sectors the three critical-infrastructure victims belong to, and neither outlet names a framework or a public administration. SRF also reports that BACS recommends installing critical updates at the latest 24 hours after their release (SRF, 2026-11-26).

item.title: GT13 holds Check Point management servers at 22 organisations; patching does not evict it, check audit logs
item.description: GreyNoise reports that an actor it tracks as GT13 had persistent access to at least 24 Check Point Security Management servers at 22 organisations in 17 named countries and territories (Switzerland is not among them), government among seven sectors, with confirmed activity from 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-02. The actor used a script for the SmartConsole authentication bypass CVE-2026-16232, which Check Point confirms and which has been fixed since July, to launch more than 100 management tasks that copied the firewall database and the internal certificate authority. GreyNoise does not know how the actor first got in or who it is, and expects the campaign to be ongoing.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-16232 +1exploitedNATOB2

GreyNoise GT13: an unattributed actor that GreyNoise believes used LLM tooling held persistent access to at least 24 Check Point Security Management servers at 22 organisations, government among them, using CVE-2026-16232 and a Rejetto HFS relay hijacked through CVE-2026-61500

GreyNoise reports an intrusion campaign it tracks as GT13 against Check Point Security Management servers: at least 22 organisations and 24 servers, confirmed activity against the Check Point servers from 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-02 and the actor's relay observed from 2026-10-02, victims in 17 named countries and territories (Germany, Austria and France among them, Switzerland not named) and sectors including government, financial services, energy and transportation (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23). GreyNoise could not determine when or how the actor first reached the Check Point servers, only that it did so before compromising the Rejetto HFS server it used as a relay; it does not attribute GT13, cannot judge motive and believes that the actor used LLM and agentic tooling (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23).

The actor ran a script for the SmartConsole authentication bypass CVE-2026-16232, purportedly adapted from the Metasploit module, to launch more than 100 management tasks, among them copying the firewall database and the internal certificate authority, minting a certificate and unloading security policies, which would disable the firewall (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23). Check Point confirmed the use of CVE-2026-16232 and called the flaw and its protections not new (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-24); the fixes are Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator R82.10 from Take 36, R82 from Take 118 and R81.20 from Take 158, and exploitation needs internet access to the management server with no restriction on Trusted Clients (Check Point, 2026-09-24); Check Point's disclosure table scores the flaw 9.3 and lists exploitation against a handful of customers with a specific configuration (Check Point, 2026-07-22). The relay was taken over by forging an HFS session cookie after recovering the signing key from login responses (CVE-2026-61500, HFS 3.0.0 to below 3.2.1) (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23; VulnCheck, 2026-07-13).

The actor planted an SSH key on its relay, and GreyNoise concludes from scp deliveries that each compromised device holds the matching private key; it also ran Nmap and a Chisel reverse proxy, used at least 30 Python scripts with victim-themed credential lists, and probed NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, vCenter, Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and domain controllers without any stated success. A bulk certificate task to 24 servers failed on each; GreyNoise notified victims directly or through government partners and expects the campaign to be ongoing (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
Any Check Point Security Management or Multi-Domain Security Management server on R82.10, R82, R81.20 or an unsupported earlier train, below the fixed Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator, whose Trusted Clients list was unrestricted, reached from the internet or from a compromised internal host.
Detection
In management-server audit logs, SmartConsole sessions authenticated by "Password based application token", which Check Point says to treat as suspicious and check for an unrecognised administrator name or address (Check Point, 2026-09-24); script-run, certificate-management and policy-unload events; outbound SSH or scp from management servers to the relay and other non-administrator hosts; unfamiliar SSH private keys and a registration in /etc/ld.so.preload, which GreyNoise says may indicate an implant; tunnelling-tool process creation. A server patched later still needs this check, reaching back to at least early October, since the actor held persistent access and copied the internal CA.
Defender takeaway
Install the fixed Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator and restrict Trusted Clients now, then treat any server with an unexplained application-token login as a compromised management plane: review policy changes and rebuild trust where the internal CA or stored credentials left.

item.title: Project Zero: one-bit change loads untrusted .NET assemblies past UMCI; fixed in October, PPL bypass expected to remain
item.description: Google Project Zero's James Forshaw shows that .NET Framework 4 falls back to a flat, non-image mapping when an assembly's executable-image header flag is cleared, so protection code that expects to check the loaded image section never sees the load, and that the code-integrity policy check meant to stop the fallback passes on Windows 11 S Mode, letting an untrusted assembly run under User Mode Code Integrity. Microsoft fixed it as CVE-2026-108398 in October 2026 (Important, CVSS 3.1 8.8, publicly disclosed, not exploited); the same behaviour bypassed VirtualBox's Windows process hardening (CVE-2026-87268) and gives code execution as a protected process light, which Microsoft's servicing criteria treat as out of scope.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-108398 +1NATOB1

Project Zero: clearing one COFF header flag makes .NET Framework 4 load an untrusted assembly past Windows code-integrity checks (CVE-2026-108398, fixed 2026-10-13); the same behaviour defeated VirtualBox's Windows process hardening (CVE-2026-87268) and is expected to remain a protected-process bypass

James Forshaw of Google Project Zero published a write-up of a code-integrity bypass found re-examining VirtualBox's Windows process hardening (Project Zero, 2026-11-23). On .NET Framework 4 the runtime first maps an assembly as an image section; if that fails with a bad-format error it falls back to a flat, data-only mapping that .NET can still run, so protection code that checks the loaded image section never sees it. A check meant to stop the fallback when code integrity is enforced tests the Windows lockdown policy for inequality with the configuration-code-integrity value, which is exactly what Windows 11 S Mode returns (User Mode Code Integrity on, Dynamic Code Security off), so it passes. Clearing the executable-image flag in the COFF header of a managed assembly, one bit with no checksum fix-up, and loading it through a .NET Framework 4 command-line utility without administrator rights ran arbitrary code under User Mode Code Integrity; it only seems to work on .NET Framework v4 (Project Zero, 2026-11-23).

Forshaw presented it at 44Con before reporting it in late September 2026, so Microsoft treated it as a zero day; CVE-2026-108398 was fixed in October 2026 by correcting the policy check (Project Zero, 2026-11-23). Microsoft rates it Important, not exploited (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-10-13).

The same behaviour defeated VirtualBox's Windows process hardening (CVE-2026-87268): an AnyCPU .NET assembly made its image screening return the bad-format status, the flat fallback loaded the unmodified assembly, and a current-user COM registration brought it into a hardened process; VirtualBox fixed it by never returning that status and by adding a COM option that disables current-user hive lookups. Against protected processes, hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads gave code execution as a protected process light without administrator rights; Microsoft's servicing criteria place such bypasses out of scope and the policy fix does not change that, so Forshaw expects it to remain bypassable (Project Zero, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
Windows hosts that rely on App Control for Business or WDAC user-mode code integrity as an application-control boundary without Dynamic Code Security (Project Zero, 2026-11-23), and Windows hosts that run Oracle VM VirtualBox 7.2.16 or likely earlier builds (Oracle, 2026-09-15).
Detection
The post says protection code that checks the loaded image section does not see this load (Project Zero, 2026-11-23); from that and the shown method, look at process creation of the .NET assembly-registration utilities with an unregister option against a file in a user-writable path, current-user COM registrations for the .NET runtime, .NET assembly loads with no matching image load, and managed assemblies whose COFF header lacks the executable-image bit.

Triage: developers and installers run the registration utilities legitimately for their own signed COM assemblies from build or Program Files paths; the discriminators are an unsigned or modified assembly, a user-writable path and a current-user COM registration on a host enforcing user-mode code integrity.

Defender takeaway
Confirm the October 2026 .NET Framework update (4.8.1 at build 4.8.9363.0, 4.8 at 4.8.4811.0, 4.6.2 to 4.7.2 at 4.7.4150.0) on every host that enforces user-mode code integrity (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-10-13) and do not treat protected process light as a boundary against local code that can run .NET Framework 4 assemblies; Dynamic Code Security blocks the behaviour but is off by default, disables loading assemblies from byte arrays and can break applications (Project Zero, 2026-11-23).

item.title: Symantec: 41 AI-authored PowerShell modules ran under an IIS web shell and exfiltrated through DNS lookups
item.description: Symantec's Threat Hunter Team found a toolkit on a stock-exchange web server in an African country in which 41 PowerShell modules ran under an IIS web shell for 3 minutes 12 seconds on 2026-09-20, hunting secrets in Group Policy Preferences, shared folders, SharePoint, SCCM and TFS, testing a guessed password, a reused token and API keys against the exchange's investment API and a securities-depository gateway, and returning their output as hex-encoded DNS lookups to a public out-of-band testing service. Symantec assesses AI authorship from the uniform scaffolding, attributes six older implants on the same server to Witchetty with high confidence but does not attribute the toolkit, and does not know whether any credential worked.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Symantec: 41 likely AI-authored PowerShell modules ran under an IIS web shell at an African stock exchange for just over three minutes, hunting secrets in SYSVOL, shared folders, SharePoint, SCCM and TFS, testing them against financial APIs and returning the output as hex-encoded DNS lookups to a public out-of-band testing service

Symantec's Threat Hunter Team found a toolkit on a stock-exchange web server in an African country: 41 PowerShell modules ran under a web shell inside the IIS worker process between 08:44 and 08:47 UTC on 2026-09-20, a new module every few seconds (Symantec, 2026-11-19). The modules profiled the host and its IIS sites and hunted for secrets in the domain's SYSVOL share (Group Policy Preferences password fields), shared policy folders, web roots and deployment directories (hard-coded passwords, AWS keys, connection strings in .xml, .json, .env and web.config files); they also searched SharePoint for the keywords aws, credential and password, queried SCCM for the machine a given user last logged on to, listed Team Foundation Server projects and probed a PostgreSQL instance and a SQL Server. Four modules tested a guessed password, a reused bearer token and several API keys against the exchange's investment API and a securities-depository gateway (Symantec, 2026-11-19).

Every module hex-encoded its output into 50-character chunks and resolved each as a DNS name under unique subdomains of a single token on a public out-of-band testing service, so the data left as DNS lookups; Symantec calls this rarely seen, cannot see the collector and does not know whether any credential or key worked (Symantec, 2026-11-19). Its case for AI authorship is uniformity: the same error handling in every module, the DNS loop copied byte for byte into all 41, generic variable names and a deliberately invalid test credential; it calls no signal conclusive (Symantec, 2026-11-19).

Symantec attributes six persistence implants on the same server to Witchetty (LookingFrog), a China-linked espionage group, with high confidence, the earliest evidence dating from April 2026, but does not attribute the toolkit to any group; it names three explanations: Witchetty with new tooling, a second operator using the same access, or an unrelated actor. The way in is not stated, a web shell under the IIS worker process suggests a vulnerability may have been exploited, and Symantec found no evidence of privilege escalation or data theft (Symantec, 2026-11-19).

Exposure
A Windows estate with an IIS server whose worker account can read secrets: Group Policy Preferences passwords in SYSVOL, credentials in web.config and deployment folders, and reachable SharePoint, SCCM and TFS servers (Symantec, 2026-11-19).
Detection
Repeated short-lived PowerShell jobs started within seconds with the IIS worker process as ancestor; DNS egress from a server-class host to long hex-looking labels under a public out-of-band testing service; reads of SYSVOL policy folders and of web.config and .env files by the web-tier account; SCCM, SharePoint and TFS queries from a web server. Symantec says the uniform scaffold and the copied DNS loop are what defenders can look for (Symantec, 2026-11-19).

Triage: out-of-band testing lookups are normal from a vulnerability scanner or penetration-test host; the discriminator is a production web server issuing them from PowerShell children of the IIS worker process.

Defender takeaway
Hunt web-tier servers for PowerShell spawned by the worker process and for server DNS egress to out-of-band testing services; remove Group Policy Preferences passwords from SYSVOL, move secrets out of web roots and shared folders, rotate any found there, and keep the web-tier account away from SCCM, TFS and SharePoint (Symantec, 2026-11-19).

item.title: F5 BIG-IP: six unauth CVSS 9.8 TMM overflows, fixed only by engineering hotfixes; check iRule and APM use
item.description: F5's 2026-11-18 notification includes six BIG-IP flaws that an unauthenticated remote attacker can use to terminate the Traffic Management Microkernel and that F5 says may allow remote code execution, each CVSS 3.1 9.8 and each needing a specific virtual-server configuration: one of five iRule commands, or an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information and Endpoint Security agents. BIG-IP 21.1, 17.5 and 17.1 are affected, no scheduled release carries the fix and F5 lists no workaround, so the fix is an engineering hotfix from F5; none of F5's advisories says the flaws are exploited.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-123637 +5NATOA2

F5 BIG-IP: six unauthenticated stack overflows rated CVSS 9.8 (CVE-2026-123637, CVE-2026-116953, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-120722, CVE-2026-121805) crash TMM and may allow code execution where an iRule command or APM policy is configured; fixed only by engineering hotfixes, no exploitation reported

F5's security notification of 2026-11-18 lists 22 advisories, 10 of them for NGINX; six BIG-IP flaws among them let an attacker without credentials crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM), disrupting traffic until it restarts, and F5 says they may also allow remote code execution (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18). All six are stack-based buffer overflows in the data plane, which processes almost all of BIG-IP's network traffic, rated CVSS 3.1 9.8 and CVSS 4.0 9.3; the management side is not exposed, and watchTowr's Sina Kheirkhah reported four of them while F5 found the other two (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18). BSI CERT-Bund's advisory, which lists only the APM flaw CVE-2026-123637, says a remote, anonymous attacker can execute arbitrary code (translated from German) (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-11-23), and NCSC-NL, whose advisory also covers six lower-rated BIG-IP flaws, rates the likelihood medium and the damage high (NCSC-NL, 2026-11-19).

Each flaw needs a specific configuration on a virtual server: an iRule that uses GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic (CVE-2026-116953); an HTTP profile with an iRule that uses PSC::ip_address (CVE-2026-120285) or MR::message route (CVE-2026-120292); an iRule that uses DNS::scrape on client traffic (CVE-2026-120722, BIG-IP DNS) or PEM::subscriber on client traffic (CVE-2026-121805, BIG-IP PEM); or an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information and Endpoint Security agents (CVE-2026-123637, APM only) (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18). BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, for some of the six, BIG-IP CNF are affected as well, and F5 checks only versions still in technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18).

No scheduled release is listed as a fix and F5 lists no workaround: the fixes are engineering hotfixes, which F5 says do not receive the QA of scheduled releases, and a system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from F5 support (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18). None of F5's advisories says the six are exploited, and they differ from CVE-2026-94127, the APM flaw F5 disclosed on 2026-09-22 that was later exploited (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18).

Exposure
A BIG-IP on the 21.1, 17.5 or 17.1 branch (BSI's product tree lists builds before the hotfix builds) whose virtual servers use one of those iRule commands or APM policy agents (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-11-23; The Hacker News, 2026-11-18).
Detection
TMM process terminations and restarts and core files in the BIG-IP system logs, tied to the virtual server that carries the affected iRule or policy, follow from the stated impact (traffic disrupted until TMM restarts); no source describes a successful code-execution chain or a post-exploitation artefact (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18).
Defender takeaway
An unauthenticated remote crash of the traffic plane, with possible code execution, can be reached only on the configurations above, so inventory those first and apply the engineering hotfix instead of waiting for a scheduled release; a system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from F5 support (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18).

item.title: N-able Mail Assure SSRF CVE-2026-134624 is on CISA KEV after a hosted-cloud breach; revoked tokens need reissuing
item.description: N-able confirmed on 2026-11-18 that an unauthorized party had reached a web server of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, the email-filtering service it runs for managed service providers, and on 2026-11-22 published CVE-2026-134624, a server-side request forgery in the LDAP-synchronisation connection check (CVSS 4.0 9.3, authenticated API user) that build 20261121.1943 fixes; CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-23. N-able says exploitation was confined to one N-able-hosted server, has not said whether the flaw was the way in, and revoked customers' API and OAuth tokens, so integrations need new credentials.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-134624exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-134624, N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts before 20261121.1943: a server-side request forgery in the LDAP-sync connection check, disclosed after a breach of N-able's hosted cloud, is listed by CISA as exploited (CVSS 4.0 9.3)

N-able disabled access to the portal and API of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, the email-filtering service it runs for managed service providers, on 2026-11-16 and confirmed two days later that it had been attacked: the intruders hit a web server and likely accessed certain credentials stored there, while email delivery kept working (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-23; The Hacker News, 2026-11-23). On 2026-11-22 N-able said it had remediated the identified vulnerability, restored the dashboard and APIs as of 2026-11-21 23:45 UTC and published CVE-2026-134624 (N-able, 2026-11-22).

The flaw: the LDAP-synchronisation connection check that runs when a relay is configured did not restrict its destination, so an authenticated API user can make the server connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, learn which are reachable and send crafted data to internal services; builds before 20261121.1943 are affected, N-able scores it CVSS 4.0 9.3 and does not claim code execution (The Hacker News, 2026-11-23; GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-11-22). CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-23 (CISA, 2026-11-23). N-able says exploitation was confined to a single N-able-hosted server and that monitoring since remediation found nothing further; it has not said whether this flaw was the attackers' way in, and it has engaged an independent forensics team and promises a root cause analysis within two weeks (N-able, 2026-11-22; The Hacker News, 2026-11-23).

N-able's response included taking the affected server offline, rotating internal platform credentials, revoking customers' API and OAuth tokens and resetting local users' passwords; it says it found no evidence that customer data, tenants' mailboxes included, was compromised and that the breach is unrelated to the N-central incident (The Hacker News, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
The Hosted Cloud is already patched and there is nothing for its customers to install; exposure runs through the MSP or hoster that serves the tenant, whose scripts and integrations stopped working when the API and OAuth tokens were revoked (The Hacker News, 2026-11-23). SpamExperts Local Cloud runs on customer hardware and the incident statements describe only the Hosted Cloud, so its operators should confirm their servers are on build 20261121.1943 (The Hacker News, 2026-11-23).
Detection
Management-plane and API audit logs for LDAP-synchronisation connection checks whose target is an internal address or a non-LDAP port follow from the stated mechanism; on the tenant side, unexplained authentication failures from integrations after the token revocation. N-able says mail flow continued throughout, so mail-flow telemetry is not expected to show the intrusion (N-able, 2026-11-22). The Hacker News notes that it is not known whether credentials the intruders may have reached were actually taken (The Hacker News, 2026-11-23).
Defender takeaway
Nothing to patch for Hosted Cloud customers; re-issue the integrations that lost their tokens, confirm the fixed build on any Local Cloud, and treat the root cause analysis due around 2026-12-06 as the point to re-check scope (N-able, 2026-11-22).
